events.title: The EU Plans to Ban Social Media For Under-13s
events.summary: The European Union has announced plans to restrict children’s access to social media across member states in a bid to free them from what President of the Commission Ursula von der Leyen described as the “capture [of] their attention, their focus, their minds” by the platforms. The proposal for a total ban on social media for children under 13 was announced in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech, where von der Leyen set out the Union’s priorities for the year ahead. It’s part of an EU Kids Act, which the Commission will unveil fully on Thursday. Children aged 13 to 15 will also not be allowed personal social media accounts but will be able to access social media through mini accounts set up and supervised by parents and guardians, with limited features, for one hour per day. Platforms will also have safe design obligations for users up to 18, with the Union planning to tackle addictive design further in the upcoming Digital Fairness Act in Autumn. “I am aware that many perceive the power of Big Tech as overwhelming and impossible to roll back. I disagree,” von der Leyen told the European Parliament. “We do not have to accept addictive features, we do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content, we do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for-AI generated sexualised images,” she added. “Europe has the power to act; it is us who decide the rules, not Big Tech.” The EU was largely expected to follow other countries in restricting children’s access to social media, which von der Leyen said has been responsible for sleep loss, anxiety, self harm, and even the deaths of European children. Seventeen of the bloc’s 27 member states are already negotiating or preparing draft legislation to protect minors online, including by setting out a minimum age to access certain services. Among those is France, whose top court last month struck down a ban on social media for under-15s because it infringed upon freedom of expression. “Cleaning up that mess, getting everyone on the same page, then running through the EU legislative process,” will probably take until 2029, expects Ashurst Perkins Coie technology lawyer Arnav Joshi. Still, he believes companies will welcome the clarity and simplicity provided by a single set of EU-wide rules. The tiered approach is designed to placate any judicial challenges by being proportionate—a rare example of where “the EU law, by not introducing a blanket ban, is perhaps even a little bit more permissive than others,” he told WIRED, referencing the sweeping social media bans in the UK and Australia . But the measures still force oversight on both guardians and the social media platforms themselves, which could risk privacy infringements. Parental monitoring could be “problematic” says Joshi, who advises global technology companies on children’s online safety, warning: “anything that has deep dive, God-mode style parental access can have a bit of a chilling effect on how children actually use that service and could have issues in terms of their own right to privacy.” The European bloc will also face similar challenges to other countries in effectively enforcing the age limits. Children in Australia have widely been able to circumvent the country’s under-16s ban on social media access. "A key issue is how to carry out the age checks and it’s not straightforward,” Joanna Conway, digital regulation partner at law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, told WIRED. Making age checks accurate, without infringing on privacy rights or harming user experience, is a challenge, she added. The EU introduced an app earlier in the year so members can prove they are over 18 and access adult-restricted sites, which it says can be applied to other age groups. Von der Leyen also acknowledged that Europeans are more widely worried by the “dizzying” speed of technology and its impact on their livelihoods and society. Artificial intelligence “has not yet delivered” value in the real economy—like factories, hospitals, and energy grids—she added, teasing initiatives that will be announced in November to address these concerns across health, transport, agri-food, advanced manufacturing, and defence and space. She also referenced the upcoming Quality Jobs Act, designed to ensure AI helps develop skills, improve the quality of jobs, and “give workers a fair chance,” and said she would invite the main artificial intelligence frontier labs for a discussion on how the EU can support industry efforts to pace the frontier. events.title: My sister and I are 10 years apart and used to hate each other. Our dynamic has totally changed over the years.
events.summary: The author and her sister have gotten much closer over the years. Courtesy of Hayley Folk For a while, I thought I'd be an only child, and I was fine with that. Then, when I was 10, my parents told me I'd soon be a big sister. My sister and I didn't get along when we were young, but our dynamic has changed over the years. When I think of my childhood, I often think of one thing: being an only child . I see myself as a blonde, curly-haired toddler who played alone with her toys. A girl who seemingly got all the attention from her parents and her family, and never, ever had to share. I never thought I'd have siblings — especially because my parents weren't even together (yes, it's complicated) and I was already 10 — until one day, when I was sat down to be told, "Hayley, you're going to be a big sister." The only problem? My little sister Hanna and I came to hate each other. Our age gap caused friction and made it hard to relate No, I'm not being dramatic. She'd agree we did, too. I'm not sure whether our mutual hatred stemmed from our 10-year age gap, the loss of my 'only child' status, or the fact that we'd often antagonize each other for no reason, as children often do, but I'd argue it was a combination of all of the above. Although research shows that large age gaps of 4+ years between siblings are becoming more common than ever, nearly 20 years ago, it wasn't quite the same. It's fair to say that we both felt out of place, freakish for not relating to each other, and lost in our own stages of life. Me: going through early stages of awkward puberty, braces, unsure if I liked boys and girls, and braving middle school. Her: a baby then outgrowing diapers, crawling into a toddler, and screaming at the top of her lungs when she didn't get what she wanted. As we grew older, we were still misaligned in our chapters. I was experiencing my first kiss, going to my senior prom, and heading off to college, while she was just turning the age I was when she was born. We fought often and unnecessarily. It didn't help that I felt the need to mother her, since our mother was struggling with addiction and ended up not being around at all. While research shows that larger sibling age gaps often lead to less intense rivalry and fewer daily conflicts , because children occupy different social and school stages, it seemed our differences just made us clash even more. Until, surprisingly to us, the last few years. The author and her sister recently took a trip together and went to a Buffy the Vampire Slayer convention. Courtesy of Hayley Folk On a trip, we realized how much our relationship had changed Over the summer, she, now 21, and I, 31, decided to take a trip to Los Angeles to attend a Buffy the Vampire Slayer convention called Hellmouth Con, together. While we frolicked around Sunnydale High, dressed in our best 90s vintage fits and odes to the characters, connecting over eating our childhood favorites from In-N-Out and arguably the best show of all time, I couldn't help but think, Wow, we've really come a long way. I even said to her, "Hanna, I feel like we're so much closer now, right?" She agreed. It could be argued that sharing my love for Buffy a couple of years ago, which she never saw on air because she wasn't born until 2004, has brought us closer together as sisters. After all, she finally understands my insatiable love for the show, my motherly tendencies toward her, and how we're basically Buffy and her little sister, Dawn, in real life. Or it could be that our dynamic has shifted from bossy big sister and annoying little sister to my being a mentor, her being my best friend, and us being each other's confidantes. Research has also shown that, as they age, large-age-gap siblings often develop mentor-mentee relationships. In the last few years, I've been able to not only encourage Hanna to follow her dreams, but also helped her move to New York City — from our small town in Southern California — from our small town in Southern California. I even helped her land a job she loves, and we see each other almost every day. It could also be that we finally understand where we each were, how we've grown, and how we can be there for one another, instead of in constant conflict. I came out as bisexual 10 years ago, so she felt comfortable coming to me when she realized her sexuality. I now see that she felt misunderstood and longed to belong as a child, just as I did. Or maybe our newfound admiration for each other is just the passage of time. After all, age differences never seem as big as we get older, right? Whatever the reason, I'm just glad we don't hate each other anymore. In fact, in a lovely turn of events, we love each other more than ever. Read the original article on Business Insider

GovCloud customers were no longer affected, but others could continue to experience severe delays, intermittent errors, and problems accessing some services or creating support cases. Salesforce said services were returning to normal in regions where the rollout had been completed. The company continues to monitor the deployment while working on a permanent fix. Salesforce said most instances were recovering as the rollout progressed. Some customers may continue to encounter errors until their instance is manually restarted, and the company has yet to confirm when the incident would be fully resolved. Salesforce said the rollout had not completed successfully on some instances, leaving customers exposed to the original problem. The company is reapplying the fix and warns that some users might need to clear cached data or restart their sessions to recover fully.

events.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
events.summary: WEF report: Progress on gender equality remains 'fragile' Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take 120 years to close. The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%. However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile." The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006. Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels. WEF Managing Director Saadia Zahidi warned that while parity is a foundation for growth and competitiveness, it is "not inevitable." "To accelerate, governments and employers need to learn from the policies that work and apply them faster. A new economy demands a new approach to talent," Zahidi said in a press release to accompany the report. Women still missing in top power roles The WEF found that women remain underrepresented in roles with the largest economic and political influence. They still hold fewer than a fifth of chief executive officer (CEO) positions, while only one in 10 ministerial roles held by women is considered high influence. While the number of ministerial roles led by women has risen 26% since 2008, only one in 10 was considered weighty then — a share the WEF report said was "virtually unchanged today." Despite nearly $1 trillion (€866 billion) being invested globally to develop artificial intelligence (AI), the report also revealed that fewer than one in five AI engineers are women, and they are underrepresented at every level of AI firms. For the 17th consecutive year, Iceland leads the ranking with 93% of the gender gap closed, followed by its Nordic neighbors Finland and Norway. The three nations have made the Top 10, along with Sweden, every year since 2006. Namibia ranked fourth globally, higher than Germany (9th), the United Kingdom (5th) and Australia (8th). The United States dropped five places in the rankings to 47th, with 74.9% of its gender gap closed. The country achieved full parity in education for a second year, ranking first in the world in that area. In the US, women have long matched men in professional and technical jobs, but parity in senior management has fallen by almost 11 points since 2006, the WEF calculated. The political score fell 4.1 points from last year after the share of women ministers dropped from two-thirds parity to one-half. The decline coincided with a lower share of women serving as Cabinet secretaries in President Donald Trump's second administration. The WEF kept the head-of-state indicator for the US at zero as the world's largest economy has never had a female president. India , the world's most populous country, remains at 131st in the rankings, with 64.5% gender parity closed. The report noted India's overall gains amount to a 4.3 percentage-point rise since 2006, which the authors said was mostly due to educational achievement. Women's labor-market participation has barely moved over 20 years, the WEF noted. India's economic parity score has varied significantly since the first report. Parity among professional and technical workers has almost doubled since 2006, to 49.9%. Among legislators, senior officials and managers, however, it is still only 13.1%. In parliament, India has closed 16.1% of the gender gap, up seven points since 2006, while the share of women in long-serving Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet has fallen recently, with parity slipping to 5.9% from a 30% peak in 2019. China , meanwhile, rose seven places to 96th, closing 69.9% of its gender gap. Economic parity is its strongest pillar, at 72.3%, but politics has barely moved in 20 years, with women still accounting for only a fraction of ministers. Namibia's rise in women's political power Large jumps for Namibia, Kenya and Ghana Reaching 84.5% parity in the latest report, Namibia leads the way in Sub-Saharan Africa, climbing four places to No. 4 in the ranking. Namibia has long been well represented by women on the political stage. Last year, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became its first female president. The country also has a female vice-president and the parliament speaker is a woman, too. Other African countries were among the biggest climbers in the 2026 rankings, with Kenya rising 33 places in a year to 65th, Ghana up 32 places to 56th and Angola climbing 30 places to 87th.

events.title: US-Canada trade war further taxes small businesses as costs rise during the Iran war
events.summary: Small business owners in the United States and Canada say a trade war between their countries is hurting sales while they are also dealing with rising expenses from higher fuel costs NEW YORK -- A trade war between the United States and Canada is making it more difficult and expensive for small businesses in the economically entwined countries to operate, according to business owners caught in the crossfire. Canada imposed reciprocal tariffs on about $20 billion (CA$27.6 billion) worth of U.S. goods last week after President Donald Trump placed import taxes on Canadian goods worth the same amount. In response to Canada's action, Trump said the U.S. also would ban imports of wine, whiskey, selected motorcycles and the dairy ingredient whey from Canada. The tariffs so far involve about 5.5% of the neighboring nations' bilateral trade in goods. Analysts say the overall economic impact therefore will be muted. But small business owners who depend on cross-border sales say a tax of up to 50% on their products and ill will created by the conflict have an outsize effect on them, especially when higher energy costs stemming from the Iran war are eroding their balance sheets. The owners of four small businesses, two in the U.S. and two in Canada, spoke with The Associated Press about the ways the trade war is affecting their companies. At Jasper Hill Farm, an artisan cheesemaker in Greensboro, Vermont, co-founder Mateo Kehler said Trump's opening salvo produced an immediate effect: canceled holiday orders from wholesale customers in Canada, whose border is only about 40 miles away. Cheese wasn't among the products made subject to new U.S. tariffs last month. Kehler suspects his hopes for expanding business in Canada are stalling because residents there resent the way the president and members of his Cabinet treat their country, a longtime ally . “The backlash on the market side is actually what’s affecting us the most,” Kehler said. “It’s the rhetoric that has inspired a boycott.” Trump has needled America’s northern neighbor repeatedly since he returned to the White House. First, it was comments last year about wanting to absorb Canada as the 51st state . After trade negotiations broke down in August, he taunted Prime Minister Mark Carney and signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. The lost sales and higher prices for materials and equipment that Kehler buys from Canada are tough to swallow when the war with Iran has made fuel for Jasper Hill Farm's trucks and machinery more expensive too, he said. Some of his suppliers and distributors are adding surcharges to cover their costs, he said. “It’s like death by a thousand cuts, because between the rising cost of energy and the tariffs, the inflationary pressure on the inputs across almost every aspect of our business — from the farming side all the way through to finished goods — is just being ratcheted up,” Kehler said. Revival Stillworks makes equipment for distilling liquor like vodka, agave and whisky and helps design spaces for producing craft spirits from the company's base on Vancouver Island, less than 20 miles from Washington state's San Juan Island. Until last month, the equipment could enter the U.S. tariff-free under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trade pact Trump negotiated during his first presidency. Now, the company's stills, fermenters and other products incur a 50% tax for crossing the border, co-founder Darcy Lane said. The customs charges are considerable because the equipment costs $250,000 to $2 million, Lane said. “We’ve got millions of dollars worth of orders that are supposed to be happening over the next four to six months, and then all of a sudden this happens again,” he said, recalling how a U.S. customer called off a project last year when Trump threatened to put tariffs on some Canadian products. Clients in the U.S. make up about half of Revival Stillworks' business. With rising oil prices during the war driving up shipping costs, many already were evaluating whether they should move forward with projects that involve imported equipment, Lane said. He and his partner are looking into other kinds of work. Since they employ engineers, welders and fabricators, their business could service the local marine industry, Lane said. “Hopefully, cooler heads prevail and everything works out, and we can continue along as business as normal," he said. “But if not, we have to put a contingency plan in place anyway." events.title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
events.summary: Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI? The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks. "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco. He accepted people were justified in being concerned about AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly. But critics say firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate, with left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, among those calling for greater governance of AI. Trump himself has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax". He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president. Altman's comments on Tuesday came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce. "It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this." But AI bosses themselves have also admitted it may be difficult to regulate a technology which is changing so quickly. In an interview with Axios published on 3 September , external , Altman said he had expected Congress to create a "basic framework" for advanced AI after his 2023 testimony, but that has yet to happen. He suggested lawmakers have struggled to keep pace with the technology and to regulate it without "slow[ing] down innovation". New safety legislation on AI is unlikely to emerge from the US Congress anytime soon, despite the fact lawmakers returned from their summer break on Monday. There is a lack of consensus within both US parties on how any regulation would happen - and the House is set to enter recess again at the end of the week ahead of the midterm elections in early November. Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Published 5 hours ago Altman's comments on Tuesday were the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked. A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing. After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X , external that every AI firm had the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards safety. "Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," the Meta chief executive wrote. "Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well." Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. Some political figures have pushed back against the view that AI firms should be able to self-regulate. Bernie Sanders said decisions about AI had been left to "a handful of the richest people in the world", while former White House strategist Steve Bannon said the public could not trust tech oligarchs to regulate themselves. OpenAI boss: 'The world is right to be afraid' Nvidia boss Jensen Huang said at the same conference on Tuesday that AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released - and not be managed by outside forces. "We don't need new laws or regulations," he said, adding there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products. Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for its hardware. Huang also argued safety is an "engineering problem" and companies should "take a pause" if they lose confidence in a product. The recent claims from inside the industry have intensified scrutiny of AI development, prompting Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to call for the pace of AI development to slow , external and urge governments to regulate the industry. The post was applauded by Altman, Google's DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk. By Tuesday, however, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement . Altman said AI companies were capable of regulating themselves. "We will get it right," Altman said, adding that if firms could not keep "alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" they would "slow down or stop". But Yoshua Bengio, one of the pioneers of modern AI, posted on X , external "ambitious efforts outside the for-profit sector" were needed to "avert the worst risks from AI".

events.title: The US government is failing Americans on AI | Shakeel Hashim
events.summary: The US government is failing Americans on AI Trump and Republicans want companies to regulate themselves. It’s a dereliction of duty that will make AI less safe I t is hard to get Sam Altman , Elon Musk and Dario Amodei to agree on much. But over the weekend, all three AI company CEOs called for AI development to slow down in the face of growing, alarming risks. Their employees are sounding the siren too, with one researcher publicly quitting and accusing OpenAI and Anthropic of “gambling with our lives”. The combination of dire warnings from insiders and growing real-world evidence of rogue AIs should, in a sane world, lead to government action. Instead, Donald Trump and the Republican leadership have their heads in the sand. On Sunday, Trump dismissed industry concerns, accusing “very negative forces” of “raising exaggerated concerns”. House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile , made it clear that Congress won’t be acting anytime soon. “They can self-police. They can self-regulate,” he said, never mind the fact that those pushing the frontier are the ones begging for legislation. In failing to act, the Trump administration and Republicans are failing the American people. The risks of AI are real: many of those developing the technology believe it is advancing far faster than their ability to control it or manage the risks. A wave of “rogue AI” incidents this summer, in which AI agents broke out of their testing environments, started collaborating with each other and ran rampage across the internet, has made fears once dismissed as “science fiction” much harder to ignore. Inside AI companies, worries of catastrophic cyberattacks, AI-enhanced bioweapons and mass unemployment are now all too commonplace. Meanwhile, companies find themselves in a classic prisoner’s dilemma. It is collectively in everyone’s interest to slow down AI development until we have a better handle on the technology. But each participant in the “AI race” has a strong incentive to defect. Collective action problems like this are nothing new. We have seen exactly the same thing with the climate crisis, where companies are not adequately incentivized to do the right thing, even though no one really wants the planet to burn. That analogy makes Trump and Johnson’s call for self-regulation all the more absurd. They are right that companies should do what’s right even without binding legislation to force them to. (Both OpenAI and Anthropic , to their credit, have indicated that they are willing to voluntarily slow down.) But relying on companies’ good intentions is a fool’s errand. The profit incentive to defect is substantial and ignoring shareholders is easier said than done. While some companies might behave themselves, not everyone will. It just takes one irresponsible actor to charge ahead and develop dangerous AI, and then we’re all in trouble. Moreover, we already have evidence that self-regulation is not working. OpenAI reportedly covered up several incidents of its models breaking out, disclosing them only after independent investigators discovered them. It freely admits that its latest model, GPT-6 Astra, is hard to monitor and control , warning users that the model might “[act] outside the user’s intended instructions” and take “harmful actions”. Anthropic, meanwhile, downplayed reports of its own AI’s problems when asked about it by a congressmember. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Situations like this are exactly why government exists: to set a floor on acceptable corporate behavior. And that is why Trump and Johnson ought to use this sudden interest in AI safety to pass concrete laws. The US government should require independent audits of the largest AI companies’ practices. It should force companies to disclose safety incidents to prevent cover ups. It should set minimum safety standards for new AI models. And the government should have the power to block the deployment of a model that does not meet those standards. Putting all this into legislation is much easier said than done, but we need not start from scratch. Good bills already exist, most notably representatives Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan’s Frontier act. If the government was serious in its duties to protect Americans, it would make passing that bill – or a version of it – a priority in the coming weeks. Trump’s argument against doing any of this is that the US is in a race with China on AI, and it must not lose. But China does not want its citizens to have their bank accounts hacked by rogue AIs, either. Rather than throw his hands up, the feted dealmaker should do what he does best: make a deal. An international treaty on minimum safety standards will not be easy – but it is still worth trying, and doing so should be the president’s highest priority at his talks with Xi Jinping this month. No company – or country – wants to cause an AI-driven catastrophe. Despite what Trump may think, it’s the government’s job to make sure they can’t.

events.title: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe | Steven Greenhouse
events.summary: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe Not only would the plan do vast economic damage – it assumes that Americans are easily bamboozled W henever Donald Trump gives a speech, it’s filled with so many lies and self-serving exaggerations that when he does utter something true, I see that as a sort of marvel. That’s what happened nearly an hour into Trump’s marathon speech last Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention, when he declared: “Only I can make this promise to you.” Trump said that just before he made a promise that was so shameless and irresponsible that what he said was indeed true: only Donald Trump could make such a preposterous promise. Feeling very generous with other people’s money, Trump promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. It certainly looked and smelled like a bribe. I guess that when you’re fearing an electoral debacle because your public approval ratings are in the toilet, because people are furious about your disastrous war of choice against Iran and because so many Americans are hopping mad that inflation has risen even though you promised to cut prices, then you might feel the need to take desperate measures, and that’s what Trump did by offering to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s pocket to help sway them to vote Republican. Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn – that’s more than the Pentagon’s budget and nearly what the US will spend on Medicare this year. Many Republicans and Trump donors rushed to criticize Trump’s $5,000 plan. Joe Lonsdale, a tech billionaire and Republican donor, said he was “strongly against bread and circus bribes ”, while Representative Bob Good of Virginia, former chair of the House Freedom Caucus, called Trump’s promise a “ socialist vote-buying scheme ”. What angers me most about Trump’s promise isn’t that it would increase the enormous $40tn federal debt even though Trump once promised to eliminate the entire federal debt . Nor am I angriest about the fact that Trump is essentially seeking to bribe the nation’s entire adult population for short-term political gain while in effect passing the cost on to our children and grandchildren. Trump is unconscionably seeking to finance his bribery by borrowing from future generations. But here is what makes me angriest: Trump evidently believes that millions and millions of Americans are such rubes that he can bamboozle them into voting Republican because they would want to get their hands on $5,000. I like to think that Americans are smarter than that and won’t be fooled. When Trump made such a shameless proposal, I couldn’t help but wonder: are there no adults in the room with Trump? Is there no one with a sense of shame or fiscal responsibility who will tell him, “Don’t offer this $5,000 bribe. It stinks to high hell, and it’s grossly irresponsible.” Some brutal mockery came from Trump’s one-time ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former House member from Georgia. She hasn’t forgotten that Trump promised last fall that thanks to his tariffs, every American, except for high-income people, would receive “ a dividend of at least $2,000” . That didn’t happen. Greene also remembers that when Elon Musk said that Doge would chop the federal budget by $2tn, Trump suggested that a sizable chunk of those savings could go directly to Americans . That didn’t happen either. Greene taunted Trump by writing on X, “ $5,000 for the peasants will be in the mail after the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.” Trump egomaniacally called the $5,000 payments a “Trump dividend”, saying the money was available “because of our tremendous strength and success economically ”. But Trump is embellishing big time here; there really hasn’t been economic success during Trump’s second term, other than the much-detested datacenter boom and the stock market hitting repeated records. Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, the trade deficit has jumped over 60% since April, the nation has lost 35,000 factory jobs since Trump’s inauguration, and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations. After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the money would come from tariff revenues , while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come from charging wealthy foreigners for visas and from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you.

events.title: Flyers are happier with U.S. airports, despite near record travel levels, J.D. Power report shows
events.summary: Overall airport satisfaction increased significantly this year, according to J.D. Power's annual North America Airport Satisfaction Study. Travelers gave higher ratings in part because of the newer gates and terminals many airports have opened in recent years, according to the study. Despite a near record number of people flying in the U.S., it appears travelers are happier with the airports they find themselves moving through. J.D. Power's annual North America Airport Satisfaction Study, released Wednesday, reported that overall airport satisfaction increased significantly this year. Travelers gave higher ratings in part because of the newer gates and terminals many airports have opened in recent years, according to the study. "Overall, travelers are happier with what they are seeing in most airports," said Mike Taylor, managing director of travel, hospitality and retail at J.D. Power. From New York's John F. Kennedy Airport to Kansas City International to Pittsburgh International, airports large and small have opened or are building new facilities to accommodate more travelers. Often, the new terminals and gates are larger, with more light and upgraded amenities, and cost billions to build. "You have to spend at least a billion to impress people," Taylor said. This is the third straight year the J.D. Power study has found an increase in airport satisfaction. The latest report is based on responses from more than 24,000 travelers. Among the largest airports, which handle more than 33 million passengers annually, Minneapolis-Saint Paul International received the top score. For airports that serve between 10 million and 32.9 million flyers annually, Tampa International was ranked No. 1, while Charleston International in South Carolina was rated the best among medium airports, which see 4.5 million to 9.9 million passengers a year. events.title: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”
events.summary: From Latin America to Southeast Asia, countries are dividing their AI investments between the two superpowers rather than choosing one over the other. Saudi Arabia celebrated the launch of what it calls the world’s most advanced Arabic-language AI model earlier this month. The technology behind it came from China even as the kingdom spends billions building its AI infrastructure with American companies. The Arabic model, Humain-m3, is based on an open-source system from Chinese startup MiniMax. Humain, the state-backed company that commissioned the model, has struck major deals with Nvidia and other U.S. technology companies to build its AI computing capacity. Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds.” Kyle Chan, fellow, John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution Saudi Arabia is not alone. From Latin America to Southeast and Central Asia, countries are buying American chips while adopting Chinese open-source models, splitting key AI projects between companies from two AI superpowers. The trend presents a growing complication for Washington’s competition with Beijing. Even countries investing heavily in American AI infrastructure are not necessarily choosing American technology for every layer of the AI stack. “Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, told Rest of World . Many countries often do not attach the same security stigma to Chinese technology that Washington does, Chan said. “Ultimately, many countries around the world want to keep their options open and not be too dependent on any single source of technology.” In August, Brazil announced an investment worth roughly $444 million into AI, which it effectively divided between Chinese and American technologies. Around $255 million will go toward supercomputing infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro, developed in partnership with China’s Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE and iFlytek. The rest, around $189 million, will go to a separate supercomputer that Brazil is currently tendering, but expecting to source from Nvidia. “The strategy is not to depend on a single company, technology or country,” President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration said in a statement , adding that the investments were intended to strengthen Brazil’s sovereignty over its data. For most countries, technological sovereignty does not mean building an entire AI stack at home, Jesse Marks, a China-Middle East research scholar at the Australian National University, told Rest of World. Competing at the frontier has become prohibitively expensive, leaving governments to decide which technologies they can develop themselves and where they must rely on foreign suppliers. For Saudi Arabia, it would be a “natural decision” to choose Chinese foundations for sovereign AI models if they perform better on relevant benchmarks, even if doing so carries political consequences with Washington, Marks said. The U.S., however, has greater leverage in parts of the stack where its technology is harder to replace, such as advanced semiconductors, networking equipment, and sensitive cloud infrastructure. But Washington will struggle with countries that want AI but cannot afford American systems or software, Marks said. “Outside of the network of American partners who are trusted or can afford it, it’s Chinese AI. It’s open models,” he said. These technological choices are also becoming intertwined with countries’ broader diplomatic relationships. “AI is one of a number of portfolios that middle powers have to consider when negotiating with a partner like the United States,” Marks said. Washington has accused Chinese labs of “free-riding” and training their models from frontier American AI models at an “industrial scale.” China, having rejected those accusations, has warned it would retaliate if Washington implements any curbs on Chinese AI companies. Chinese companies are ramping up efforts to compete with American companies on different layers of the AI stack. In Egypt, Huawei has bid to build AI data centers for the government, according to a source-based report by Bloomberg, competing against a proposal involving Nvidia. A successful bid would give Chinese companies another foothold in a market where AI infrastructure has so far been dominated by American technology. Southeast Asia is another region where China-U.S. competition over technological influence is increasingly apparent. Washington launched the U.S.-ASEAN AI Spark initiative in July, offering financial and technical support to Southeast Asian governments interested in adopting American AI technologies for public-sector use.

events.title: Great news for sneaky people: iOS 27 lets you secretly hide your location sharing
events.summary: Apple's location-sharing feature in iOS 27 now lets you hide your location sharing. Katie Notopoulos Now you can temporarily "Hide My Location" on iPhones instead of fully revoking a contact's permission. The other person won't be alerted; it just looks like your phone is off or in bad cell service. This is great for planning a surprise party, or…. lots of other stuff. Apple's new privacy feature is sure to be welcome news for anyone up to sneaky things. The iPhone's new iOS 27 update has a new feature that allows you to temporarily hide your location from someone you're sharing it with — without sending them an alert. Previously, if you stopped sharing your location, that person would get a little gray update in the iMessage chain you had with them (this wouldn't be delivered like a new text, but it would be noticeable if they looked at your text exchange). Just tap that "Hide My Location" button When you click into someone's name in your contacts who you are currently location sharing with, you can hit "Hide My Location". Katie Notopoulos / Business Insider Now, if you hit "Hide location" for a specific person, it won't send that notification anymore. Instead, they'd only notice if they specifically went to find you on their map or in Find My. And then, it would simply say "No location found" and "Off-Network" — as if your phone was turned off or you were in an area with no cell service. This is what it looks like when someone has hidden their location from you: It just looks like your phone is off or out of network when you do "Hide location." Katie Notopoulos / Business Insider Previously, people would get alerted if you stopped sharing: Previously, you stop location sharing, the other person will see an alert that you did so. Katie Notopoulos / Business Insider Apple's announcement says that this feature is great for things like planning a surprise party for someone. Sure! Yes, that's exactly what I was thinking of. There are, of course, plenty of good and above-board reasons you might want to temporarily hide your location. When discussing this with my editor, he recalled how he had physically turned off his phone while running a proposal-related errand — instead of ending location-sharing with his girlfriend (now fiancée) — so as not to ruin the surprise. Revoking location-sharing isn't always so simple There's a divide between Gen Z and older people where location sharing is much more normalized among the youths (if you're horrified by the idea of sharing your location, you may be old). Plenty of people share their location with a large group of friends — and while they do so, thinking it's fine most of the time, everyone does stuff they want some privacy for. A doctor's visit, a job interview, or who knows what. Not my business! Of course, we can't forget how Scheana Shay in the later-era "Vanderpump Rules" used her friend Katie Maloney's location-sharing to discover that she had spent the night with a male bartender and former castmate, much to everyone's surprise. For friend groups that are promiscuous with their location sharing, it may seem like a passive-aggressive or pointed gesture to stop sharing your location entirely. This allows people to quietly go dark for a bit. There's also a safety aspect here: in abusive situations, alerting a partner or other unsafe person that you're stopping location sharing could put you at risk. But there are a few obvious groups of people who will be thrilled by this new development. Teenagers whose access to an iPhone is contingent upon location sharing are probably delighted by this new ability to evade curfews or skip soccer practice to hang out at the mall without their parents noticing. And on r/adultery , there's much celebration. "This is the most exciting thing I've read since they unveiled hidden apps 3 years ago!" one commenter wrote about the announcement. "Now if I can get my car to do the same thing…" wrote another. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Gulf’s female startup ecosystem is flourishing. So, where’s the funding?
events.summary: Welcome to this week’s Fortune Gulf Brief. We’ll be covering:   Why the Gulf’s startup industry is missing half the picture   Geopolitical tensions fail to diminish UAE’s appeal among wealthy expats  Abu Dhabi’s Yas Island gets $3.3 billion boost   How the UAE is putting billions to work—from German AI to Indian aluminium  And, the three we enjoyed reading this week (including the launch of the 2026 Fortune 500 Europe ranking )  As I reported last week, the Middle East and North Africa region’s gender funding gap remains stark , with male-founded startups accounting for more than 96% of the $375 million in capital that was deployed in August.   Female-founded startups secured just $8.5 million with a total of two transactions.   It made for puzzling reading, given that the region’s startup ecosystem, particularly in the Gulf, is thriving, with more women choosing to launch their own businesses.  Abu Dhabi alone recorded 3,058 new business licenses issued to Emirati women in the first half of 2026 , highlighting the growing role of women entrepreneurs in the emirate’s economy.   So, I decided to dive deeper into the topic to gain clarity on why the disparity persists and spoke to several key players in the ecosystem to help me do so.   What quickly became apparent was the underrepresentation of women allocating capital.   “Gulf investor networks are still very male-dominated, especially at decision-making levels,” Lucy Chow, who serves as secretary general in the UAE office of the World Business Angels Investment Forum and as a limited partner at U.K.-based Pact VC, told me. “That matters—because deal flow follows networks.”  That’s not to say that progress isn’t being made on the ground.   In May last year, Aliph Capital, the Gulf’s first women-founded private equity firm, closed its debut fund at $200 million. Aliph Fund I will invest $15 million–$40 million in Gulf-based companies across high-growth sectors, providing capital to drive scale and operational efficiency.  In recent years, both the UAE and Saudi Arabia have been particularly proactive in making capital more accessible.  The TiE Women MENA Program 2026 marks the 7th edition of the regional initiative by TiE Dubai , which aims to mentor and fund women-led startups across the region. The Women in Tech Accelerator, orchestrated globally by Standard Chartered and executed regionally via partners such as the UAE’s Village Capital and Saudi Arabia’s Falak Holding, has often served as the primary financial lifeline for early-stage female-led tech startups.  Last week, Standard Chartered and Falak Holding awarded three Saudi women-led start-ups equity-free grant funding totaling $45,000 in Riyadh. On 28-29 September, Riyadh will host the Women Shaping Wealth Summit 2026 , bringing together an influential community of investors, founders, business leaders, policymakers, and innovators.  Alongside its main-stage discussions, the summit will host a Live Demo Day connecting female founders with investors, dedicated startup and founder showcases, curated speed networking, mentorship and peer sessions, and structured opportunities for investors, entrepreneurs and leaders to forge meaningful connections.  You can read my full article here . Melissa Hancock As ever, thanks for reading, and do keep in touch with your thoughts and ideas. melissa.hancock@fortune.com   This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ladbrokes owner prepares to cut 400 jobs weeks after profit boost
events.summary: Entain, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, starts consultation process over customer care roles The Ladbrokes owner, Entain, has said it is preparing to cut 400 jobs, only weeks after the FTSE 100 business reported better than expected profit in its first half of the year. The gambling group, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, has started a consultation process that could remove one in five of its 2,000 customer care jobs. Its chief executive, Stella David, said the proposed changes were made to ensure the “business remains competitive, financially resilient, and well positioned for the future as our sector faces an increasingly challenging operating environment. “This decision has not been made lightly, and our immediate priority is to support those of our colleagues who may be impacted through this transition.” It comes only weeks after the company revealed its underlying operating profit had hit £479m in the six months to the end of June – 2% below the same period in the year prior but ahead of what investors had expected. Entain blamed the job cuts partly on higher taxes in the UK, as the sector also braces for a mooted increase to machine games duty in the budget. The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly looking at increasing the levy in his inaugural budget on 28 October, in a way that could target betting shops and adult gaming centres (AGCs). AGCs, which offer 24-hour gambling machines, have grown rapidly across UK high streets in recent years, disproportionately targeting economically deprived areas . While online casinos were hit with a tax increase in Rachel Reeves’s budget last year, duty on physical slot machines in AGCs were not affected. Doubling machine games duty could increase the tax take from “category B” £2-a-spin slot machines by between £275m and £458m, on top of the £600m they currently pay, according to research by the Social Market Foundation thinktank . David wrote to Andy Burnham last week, arguing that doubling the standard rate of machine games duty from 20% to 40% would add about £100m to the cost of running Entain’s retail business in the UK, and claiming that could result in 1,470 betting shop closures in the UK and 15,900 job losses. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Burnham has previously backed a proposal by Gordon Brown to pay for an end to the two-child benefit cap by tapping the gambling industry for more tax. Entain, which is headquartered in London and employs more than 28,000 people worldwide, started as GVC Holdings in 2004 under Kenny Alexander. It has grown into one of the biggest betting businesses in the world, and includes brands such as BetCity and Eurobet as well as gaming brands Foxy Bingo, Gala and PartyCasino.

events.title: CEOs are still betting on the leadership trait AI can’t replace
events.summary: In today’s CEO Daily: Leaders haven’t forgotten the value of a good boss. The big leadership story: The new Fortune 500 Europe is out today. The markets: Stocks rebound ahead of the Fed’s rate decision. Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . Good morning. I did not expect to return from the Yale CEO Caucus in Washington yesterday feeling more hopeful than when I arrived. After all, this is day 200 of the Iran War, which has killed thousands, exposed security gaps , cost U.S. taxpayers at least $42 billion , and sparked global protests amid rising fuel costs. There’s concern about the economy, the markets, jobs, climate, compute, and the state of the union, not to mention OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei pondering whether their products will kill us all. Where’s the hope in that? While the semiannual gathering of CEOs, policymakers, journalists and scholars hosted by Professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, founder of the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute, is off the record, I can share some polling data and feedback from private conversations. Here’s what stuck with me: A shared desire for common ground and rule of law. I didn’t meet anyone, left or right, who disagreed with the Supreme Court decision to reject President Trump’s plan to make it harder to vote by mail. There were standing ovations for former Vice President Mike Pence, who was honored with the Yale Patriot Public Service Award for Executive Leadership, and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who received the first Yale Patriot Public Service Award for Legislative Leadership. What unites them isn’t their politics but their commitment to the Constitution, public service, integrity and something bigger than themselves. A shared celebration of the importance of human leadership. The value of a good boss isn’t always clear from the rhetoric, especially among tech leaders who love to vilify managers as useless layers of bureaucracy in an era of always-on agents. While AI might eliminate redundant roles, it doesn’t diminish the value of a great manager any more than it reduces the value of a great teacher. What drove that home for me was the praise for Corning CEO Wendell Weeks, who was honored with the Yale Legend in Leadership Award. It’s clear from those comments and my podcast conversation with Weeks that the most important factor in making him one of the most transformative leaders in Corning’s 175-year history isn’t his technical prowess but his ability to inspire excellence, loyalty, and respect. A shift in the conversation around AI . There’s an interest in addressing fears about the technology: 88% of respondents in a flash poll said Trump should address AI safety with Chinese leader Xi Jinping when they meet next week; 74% think he’ll do it. And 93% of attendees disagreed with Trump’s Truth Social post that AI warnings are a hoax. The fears of rogue agents know no boundaries. If the U.S. and China can find some common ground around safety and regulation, we could all be better off. events.title: A candidate brought her toddler to an interview. It didn't bother me — and she got the job.
events.summary: Recruiter Jalonni Weaver is a parent and says she approaches candidates with the understanding she'd want if she were job-hunting. Courtesy of Jalonni Weaver Recruiter Jalonni Weaver says job candidates shouldn't be penalized when life gets messy. She said she advanced a job seeker who interviewed alongside her toddler because the woman did well. Weaver says communication matters most and that she tries to put herself in every candidate's shoes. Jalonni Weaver is an in-house recruiter at a life insurance company in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. She's worked in the field since 2021. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. I was interviewing a candidate for an early-career role. We got on the call, and she introduced herself, then moved the camera. She was like, "My toddler's sitting right here eating. Is it OK? He's not going to be a problem." She explained that she couldn't afford childcare because she was unemployed. Her toddler wasn't a problem. I have a one-year-old, and she's a problem. Most of the time, her toddler was just eating. He would make noises every now and then, but we were able to get through the full interview. I've been unemployed with a kid. Thankfully, I could still provide because I had a significant other, but I understood where she was coming from. People face challenges. Not every applicant may have a strong WiFi signal. Not every applicant may have a super quiet environment. I've had several times when people have been interviewing from their cars or from closets. I don't really look at where you are because I try to put myself in everybody's shoes. I'm like, "In this market, if you're doing this, you need a job ." I try to look at the bigger picture and not flag people just because they're not in a suit sitting at a desk. I try to look at it from a human lens rather than, "You'll get docked because you had to reschedule your interview because you're in the hospital." That doesn't mean there are no red flags. If someone reschedules and reschedules, I'm sending an email asking, "Hey, is there something going on? Are you still interested?" If somebody doesn't show up, I'll send one email and say, "If you would like to reschedule, here's the link." It's all about communication . The people who show up with their kids or interview in their cars are making an effort. In this case, I moved the woman forward in the process because she did well, not because I felt pity for her. For the second round , she came in person to interview with a panel after finding someone to watch her son. After her interview with the team, they said they wanted to hire her. A couple of hours later, I called her with the good news. I knew she was with her toddler again because I could hear him in the background. I told her she got the role, the pay, and that they enjoyed meeting her. She was ecstatic. After she got the offer, she said it would allow her to look into childcare. She's also moving closer to the office. That matters because in Dallas, if you live in a suburban area, and you're coming into a busier area, it's going to take you a good minute to get here. If you're getting off at 5 o'clock, you don't want to have to rush across town before day care closes. There are so many things that happen in life, and you don't realize what a small gesture of being human can do. Since I have a toddler, too, I know that feeling as a mom: You just want to provide for your child. When she found out she got the job, you could hear the relief in her voice, like she was thinking, "I can finally start living again and doing what I need to do." events.summary: Rotherham has 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people but there are 288 in Cotswold district council area Young people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable opportunities in Britain, according to a report that warns stark regional divisions are fuelling a crisis in youth work. As ministers push to combat rising youth unemployment, the analysis from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) showed young people faced a tougher challenge in some parts of the country to find work than in others. Publishing a new “local youth opportunity index” to track job vacancies across Britain, it said there was a sixfold gap in jobs in the South Yorkshire town compared with the more affluent Cotswolds, where there are fewer young adults but more opportunities. Whereas Rotherham has 46 online job vacancies for every 1,000 young people, there are 288 in the area covered by Cotswold district council. Highlighting deep regional divisions, the report found nine of the 10 best areas for youth job opportunities are in the south of England. Places with job openings relative to the local youth population below the national average of 109, include East Renfrewshire in Scotland, Newcastle-under-Lyme in Staffordshire, and Broxtowe in Nottinghamshire. Cities including Sheffield , Coventry and Cardiff also ranked near the bottom of the list for youth employment opportunities. Places with the most opportunities included Woking in Surrey, Gloucester, Cherwell in Oxfordshire, and Warrington in the north-west of England . The analysis comes as ministers await recommendations from a highly anticipated report by Alan Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness . The former Labour health secretary, who is expected to publish his findings next month before the autumn budget, has called for a policy overhaul involving education, welfare and employment support. Britain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neet) surpassing 1 million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade. Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill health and a tough jobs market. The IPPR said its report showed that becoming Neet was not simply a question of an individual’s qualifications or willingness to look for work. It urged ministers to prioritise overhauling the apprenticeship system and to create a new “work start” programme that would fund youth jobs in areas with too few entry-level opportunities. It also called for a new “youth allowance” that would replace different rates of universal credit benefits based on work capability. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Responding to the IPPR report, David Blunkett, the former Labour education secretary, said he had first-hand experience of the challenges facing young people from growing up on a Sheffield council estate and leaving school at 16 with no qualifications. “Young people have an immense amount to give. With national ambition, local leadership and the willingness to invest, we can ensure that birthplace does not determine a young person’s future,” he said. “We can renew the promise that should lie at the heart of any decent society: that no young person will be discarded, that the door to opportunity will remain open and that everyone will have the chance to build a life of purpose.” A government spokesperson said: “Where you’re from should never determine where you end up in life. “The Milburn review will lay the foundation for further youth employment reform, but thanks to our £2.5bn investment, we are already taking action, including reprioritising apprenticeships for young people and rolling out youth hubs to every community, helping us create 1m work and training opportunities. “We are also supporting businesses to back young talent by offering hiring incentives worth up to £8,000 and continuing the national insurance exemptions for under-21s and apprentices under 25.” UK unemployment and employment statistics

events.title: An aging Congress attempts to regulate AI without using it
events.summary: Members of Congress and governors are under increasing pressure to regulate AI , but more than two dozen of them who spoke with Axios said they don't use the technology or have rarely done so. Why it matters: That striking admission — particularly among older, influential lawmakers — comes amid calls for an AI slowdown and warnings within the industry that it could end humanity if left unchecked. Critics argue that it's impossible for politicians to grasp how rapidly the technology is changing — and the threats or scientific breakthroughs it might unleash — if they don't use it or even dismiss it. One House Democrat called it "f*cking absurd," arguing, "Anyone who's overseeing this has to be someone who's a regular user." "That's a real problem," said Rob Flaherty, a 35-year-old Democratic digital strategist who co-founded a group to push his party to move faster in confronting AI. "Understanding what it can do is essential to figuring out what we ought to do about it." "As we begin to legislate on issues related to AI, it helps to have experience using it," said Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), who's 47. Zoom in: Several lawmakers, including those steeped in seniority and in charge of key committees, told Axios they simply haven't tried AI. "Heavens no," said Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, when asked if he uses AI. "Personally? I don't think I've ever used it," said Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), 74, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee. "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating." "I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair. On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that she needs a "primer on AI, and now with the scare that we have out there, it's much more important to be engaged." A GOP senator, speaking anonymously to offer candid remarks about their colleagues, told Axios that the number who use AI is "not very high." That's helped lead to a knee-jerk negative reaction toward AI among several lawmakers, the senator added, as polls show growing numbers of voters turning against it. Some elected officials said they don't utilize AI much personally, though some on their teams employ the technology. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), who's 48, said he uses AI "on the Google, when you can get a little bit of that search summarized for you. But otherwise no. I do not use it in research. We do not use it in our writing." He said that he supports robust regulation and though some in his state government use AI, final decisions must be made by humans. Other politicians were unsure if they've ever used AI — or said they've only done so by accident. "I don't think I do," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), 70, when asked if he utilizes it. "If I Google something, it kicks off an AI thing, but that's about as far as I go." "I don't know. I can't remember," said Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), 88. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), 73, said she doesn't seek out AI on her own, but that "it pops up on my phone occasionally." "Not intentionally," said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), 68. "The only AI use that I'm kind of familiar with is an AI tool attempting to summarize email chains, and they often get it wrong." What they're saying: Some lawmakers such as Kaine argued that they don't need to use AI to write legislation about it. He said he has read a lot about it and trusts his judgment more than AI. After we spoke with him, Pallone shared a statement through a spokesperson that said: "You don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated. Members of Congress don't need to spend their time talking to AI chatbots all day to know we need to rein in this dangerous technology." Friction point: But some members of Congress were irked or surprised that colleagues don't use a technology they're seeking to regulate. "Are you serious?" Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), 74, said in response to our question. "I use it for everything! I can't believe there's a senator that doesn't use AI." Yes, but: There are members of Congress who are frequent AI users, including some in Hickenlooper's age range. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, told Axios he uses AI "every day." Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), 76, went back to school to get a master's degree in machine learning and said he prefers Claude. Catch up quick: Some of the most powerful elected officials in the country have told other media outlets in the recent past that they don't use AI. In late 2025, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), 54, said in an interview that he didn't think he'd ever used AI. About the same time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to President Trump, 80, said that she didn't think Trump personally uses AI, though his social media account regularly posts AI-made content.

events.title: The things Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg allow — and forbid — their daughter to vibe code
events.summary: Priscilla Chan said she limits what her daughter can vibe code. Taylor Hill/Getty Images Priscilla Chan said she doesn't let her daughter vibe code products that are "open to the internet." "She wanted to build a dating site," Chan told Colossus. "That was a no." Mark Zuckerberg and his wife have long limited their children's access to technology. Mark Zuckerberg's daughter is vibe coding. Her mom isn't vibing with the open web. The Meta CEO has long set tech restrictions on his children. In 2019, he told Fox News that he liked that his kids could video chat with their extended family, but didn't want them to sit in front of a computer "for a long time." We're now in the age of AI, and the Zuckerbergs — like parents everywhere — have a whole new technology to contend with. In a Monday profile about her husband in Colossus , Priscilla Chan showed Jeremy Stern her daughter's account on Replit, a vibe coding platform . While she lets her daughters explore, Chan said she limits the kinds of apps they can build. "She's quite limited, because Mom doesn't let her build things that are open to the internet," Chan said. Chan walked through some of her daughter's vibe-coded creations, like a messaging app. There were also apps similar to GeoCities and the game FarmVille , according to Colossus. Like her father, Zuckerberg's daughter seems to have an entrepreneurial spirit. Each app included a plan for marketing and sales plan. Other things were off limits. "She wanted to build a dating site," Chan said. "That was a no." Zuckerberg's children have long been experimenting with AI tech. In 2024, he said that his daughter was 40 pages into writing a novel about "mermaid crystals" with AI-generated images. (It's not immediately clear which of Zuckerberg's three daughters was vibe coding. August, their middle child, wrote the mermaid book.) Chan isn't alone in limiting her daughter's access to the web. Google CEO Sundar Pichai didn't give his middle-school-aged kid a phone, and Mark Cuban set up special routers to monitor his kids' internet usage at home. The tech tradition dates back to Steve Jobs , who famously didn't let his kids use the iPad he helped create. Meta is investing big in AI, pouring more and more cash into the expansion of its computing power. The company has its own vibe coding product , which it announced in August, as well as the new personal agent Muse. Zuckerberg said he used Muse to find kid-friendly recipes . For the record, Zuckerberg doesn't seem to be pushing his daughter's vibe coding. "He didn't tell her to do any of this," Chan told the publication. "It's been all on her own," she added. events.title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
events.summary: For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China, and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous , tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down. “Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “ We Must Pace the Frontier .” China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal. “The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.” Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies. “His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.” Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”) The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained. When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fear-mongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.” The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power. “Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.” In a recent essay , China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs. “Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.
