events.title: Why Keppel DC REIT runs its data centres like shopping malls: CEO
events.summary: Managing Keppel DC REIT is about strategising the right mix of tenants to ensure sustainable long-term growth, says Loh Hwee Long, chief executive of the REIT manager. Keppel DC REIT uses a hybrid tenant model mixing long-term hyperscaler contracts with shorter colocation leases to drive higher yields and sustainable growth amid the AI-driven data centre boom. The REIT focuses on mature, high-barrier markets like Singapore, Japan, and South Korea, leveraging local expertise and strategic acquisitions to capitalise on strong demand and pricing power. Singapore serves as a key digital hub with robust connectivity and capital support, while Keppel DC REIT offers lower-risk, steady returns compared to volatile tech stocks, attracting more informed investors. SINGAPORE – For most people, the term data centre brings to mind endless rows of cabinets filled with black boxes and blinking lights, housed inside a vault-like windowless building with few human beings. It sounds like a mundane and soulless real estate business. But there is so much more to a data centre operator than just keeping the servers on 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Managing a portfolio of these buildings as a successful and profitable real estate investment trust (REIT) means operators have to look beyond simply offering real estate space and sustainable energy solutions to attract customers, as most data centres are already offering them as table stakes. But as the global AI boom sends tech stocks soaring, data centre REITs are also facing tougher questions from investors about their yields and risk-adjusted returns. For Keppel DC REIT, the answer lies in strategising the right mix of tenants to ensure sustainable long-term growth, Loh Hwee Long, chief executive of the manager of the REIT, said in an interview with The Straits Times. Securing contracts with hyperscalers – tech giants that operate large-scale cloud networks – may seem like a stable source of income, but it may not be the most lucrative as such single-tenant contacts are usually locked in for as long as 15 years at the minimum, he points out. To ensure its portfolio continues to benefit from the growing demand for data centres, Keppel DC REIT leases only around 30 per cent of its assets on long contracts. The rest of its tenants are on shorter leases, renting the space and facilities from the operator for their own server hardware, a practice known as colocation. Loh likens this hybrid model of hyperscaler contracts and colocation to the anchor tenant model of a shopping mall. “Actually, it’s just like VivoCity,” Loh chimes, pointing to the shopping centre down the road from Keppel’s office at Harbour Front. “The 30 per cent is basically your anchor tenant, like a supermarket or department store, where the rates are a bit lower and not too interesting from a growth perspective. Then you’ve got the smaller pop-up stores that you can really drive up the yield with much higher rents.” However, unlike a sprawling mall like VivoCity, Keppel DC REIT’s data centres do not house a highly diverse mix of tenants. Instead, Keppel DC REIT complements its mix of hyperscalers primarily with larger customers such as financial institutions and government bodies. The focus on this unique sub-segment gives the data centre operator more levers to drive organic growth, Loh said. “It’s no longer about 1 per cent to 2 per cent annual growth, it can be more. And that becomes our differentiator.” Hyperscalers accounted for half the group’s top 10 clients, according to its results for the first half of 2026 ended June 30. The top unnamed client was a hyperscaler contributing 43.5 per cent of the portfolio’s total rental income of $210.4 million. Meanwhile, the biggest non-hyperscaler tenants contributed about 15 per cent. This strategy is also more suited for the markets that Keppel DC REIT is primarily operating in. While its portfolio includes data centres in Europe and Australia, it sees Singapore, Japan and South Korea as the key “tier one” markets. Keppel DC REIT announced on Sept 1 its acquisition of two freehold colocation data centres in the Greater Tokyo area for around $1.5 billion, taking its assets in the country to five. Loh noted that market conditions in Japan, Singapore and South Korea would allow the REIT manager to capitalise on strong demand and act as a price-setter for higher rents. These are mature markets that have not only deep fibre connectivity and established hyperscaler clusters, but also high barriers to entry for new data centre operators due to supply constraints arising from a lack of land and power. According to Loh, building a new data centre in Japan could take five to seven years, as the suspension of nuclear power has compounded energy constraints, while challenges in the construction sector could cause further delays.

events.title: Trump escalates war on federal data
events.summary: The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government. Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation. Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats. Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data. 🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases. The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles. Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic. 🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy , NPR reported . The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies. The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute . ⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported . For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws. The EEOC is now planning to do away with the so-called EEO-1 reports, which require companies to provide data on their workforces broken down by race, ethnicity, sex and job title. The move comes amid a broader Trump administration crackdown on DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — initiatives. At a July hearing, Andrea Lucas, an EEOC commissioner appointed by Trump, said the data collection was burdensome for employers and encouraged discrimination against white workers, per the Guardian. What they're saying: "The level of politicization in this administration is beyond anything I've seen," says Denice Ross, former U.S. chief data scientist and currently director of the Data Policy Institute at the Federation of American Scientists. "I've been doing this work for 25 years." Zoom out: Fears about the handling of data that doesn't comport with Trump's worldview have been around for years . Last year, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics hours after the agency released disappointing jobs numbers. "Today's Jobs Numbers were RIGGED in order to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad," Trump wrote. The Department of Homeland Security has stopped regularly publishing comprehensive immigration enforcement statistics, including data that allowed outsiders to assess the administration's deportation efforts. The official who oversaw DHS's independent statistics office resigned in July, The Atlantic reported . According to a tracker run by former federal government data scientists, 38 datasets have been eliminated since Trump returned to office. Hundreds of other datasets have been altered or disrupted. The other side: "The Trump administration is committed to providing the American people with timely, accurate, and relevant data that's helpful to inform meaningful research, discourse, and decision-making," White House spokesman Kush Desai said. "Ensuring public health and other critical data actually reflect reality while refusing to waste taxpayer resources on ideological pet projects are all important parts of that mission." The bottom line: "We really take data for granted," Ross said. "It's invisible infrastructure, like a bridge or cell service. We don't notice until it's gone."

events.title: I quit my Google software engineering job and became a watercolor artist. Here’s how I’m using — and not using — AI.
events.summary: Watercolor artist Sara Wilczynska explains how she uses AI to help her with her business — and where she draws the line with the technology. Courtesy of Sara Wilczynska Sara Wilczynska is a Google software engineer turned watercolor artist in San Diego. She uses AI to help her as a business owner with planning, bookkeeping, copyediting, and coaching. However, she says she has a clear boundary of not using AI to generate any of her actual artwork. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sara Wilczynska, a 41-year-old watercolor artist and founder of Swil Arts who lives in San Diego. Prior to her art career, she worked as a software engineer in the finance and tech industries before quitting her job at Google in 2022. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I started using AI pretty early on. I founded my art studio in 2023 — after quitting my software engineer job at Google the year prior — which was when generative AI started to become more accessible and powerful. In a way, I was growing my studio with it, and having a tech background made me more prone to experiment, be excited, and feel less scared of it. However, I was always very clear that I never wanted AI to replace me at the core and the heart of my business. I wanted to create and to add value to people's lives through my creativity. Still, I identified that there are many things involved in running a business that require time, energy, and money, which AI can really help reduce friction with. I believe there's a way for artists and creatives to work with AI, and it can hopefully help us redefine the value we add as artists and creatives. Here's how I do and don't use AI. How I don't use AI I'd never use AI to generate any artwork. I've always had a very clear boundary around that — I'll never use AI for art creation, ideation, creative brainstorming, and visual storytelling. From the beginning of my art career, I've used traditional media — ink, watercolor, brushes, and paper. Even if I digitize it later in order to put it on products, the heart of it is creating everything in a traditional way with hands and traditional mediums. Sara Wilczynska says she will never use AI in the creation of her art. Courtesy of Sara Wilczynska I saw a lot of potential and value in the human aspect of it, like sketching on location and capturing with all the senses. AI can process an image, but it's not going to have that experience or perspective or interpretation or locality — all the things that a human adds . I have a weekly newsletter where I share updates from the studio, in which I also sprinkle in what I call "California moments worth keeping." These are different snapshots of Southern California life that I sketched, as well as a little story of the inspiration. I wouldn't go to AI and say, "Come up with a 'California moment worth keeping' for my newsletter," because that's not authentic. The whole point is that it's my lived experience. Much of Wilczynska's art is centered on San Diego and Southern California. Courtesy of Sara Wilczynska How I use AI in my art business When I've already captured the moment, sketched it, taken pictures of my sketches, and have the story behind it, I feel OK for AI to proofread or edit my newsletter and to suggest a better flow of sentences, because I'm not a copywriter. I treat AI almost like a voice recorder. Often, I'll come up with the thoughts, topic, and content that I want to write, and speak it to my phone while I'm lying down or commuting. My stories and content are my own, though. I also have a few custom-trained GPTs that are very helpful for my art business. First of all, I trained my own personal art coach. I defined my signature style, artistic voice, and values, and once I finish an artwork, I feed it to the custom GPT and ask for feedback and criticism. That's been very helpful for my growth as an artist and as a creator. I trained another AI agent to help me to filter art opportunities, like grants, residencies, and contests. It would be a full-time job to go through and see which ones I'm eligible for and that resonate with my work. I periodically feed my agent a list of different opportunities, and it can do the first layer of filtering because it already knows me, my business, and my criteria. I also sometimes use AI to help me with reference photos. If I'm doing my own art, I can usually paint on location, but if I'm working for a client, I'm sometimes unable to take my reference photos; for example, if the piece is going to be a surprise for someone, such as a house portrait, I shouldn't go there and start photographing it. In those cases, AI can help me figure out things like a good light source or a good architectural perspective for the limited reference photos I might be working from. I'd estimate that AI easily saves me at least 20 hours of work a week I use it for things that many business owners use it for — strategizing, long-term planning, and bookkeeping. I might have specific questions about QuickBooks, or some legal questions about intellectual property. I also use it for research and fact-checking. When I work on a project where the storytelling and meaning are very important, it's good to validate botanical, symbolic, architectural, geographical, or historical details. Since I'm not a photographer and don't have professional equipment, I also use it for mock-ups and fixing photos. In the past, I'd use Photoshop, but it's easier to talk to AI and give it a prompt to put the product against a nice background and fix the lighting. I've developed quite a lot of patience with the iterative process of prompting — and I sometimes even create my prompts with AI. My process has definitely changed and is evolving as the tools are too. When I first started using AI, it was super crappy and hallucinated much more. It wasn't reliable, and it would go into stupid loops. It's only in the last six to 12 months that it can actually do things quite well and reliably. I have concerns, but I take a middle path with AI Because of my technical background, I take a balanced approach and have a healthy skepticism about AI. I don't want to glorify it, while also not scapegoating it as the most terrible thing ever. Exercise, rest, daily walks, and being in nature help me keep my nervous system regulated, which helps counterbalance the pull of technology. A journal prompt created and painted by Wilczynska. Courtesy of Sara Wilczynska I definitely have some worries or concerns about AI on a broader scale, such as the environmental impact , which I hope is getting more and more scrutinized by the right people. With the pace of development of AI, I'm sometimes worried that ethical or legal considerations aren't developing at the same pace, in terms of consent, training, copyright, and how AI is used for things like deepfakes . My tech background makes me really understand and keep treating it as a tool that, like any tool, can be used either cons

The reports began appearing on BT's community forums over the weekend, with customers describing sudden bursts of PIN messages arriving within minutes despite them making no attempt to reset their passwords. One customer said they received between 50 and 70 PIN texts "in the space [of] a few minutes," while a second reported more than 100. A third said the number had passed 500, and another claimed to have received more than 1,000 . One BT customer who contacted The Register separately said they had received around 300 password reset emails over the previous 24 hours, typically arriving in bursts of around 50 within a minute before stopping for several hours. BT has acknowledged the problem but has yet to explain what is behind it. "We are aware that some customers have received a large number of password reset pin messages and we are actively investigating the cause of this," a BT moderator said on the company's community forum. "If you have received multiple messages like this, please ignore them and remain vigilant for any unusual activity with further messages or unexpected calls." BT added that customers' email accounts are secure and that those receiving the messages do not need to take any action. At least one customer, however, claims someone accessed their account during the PIN barrage. The user said they lost access to both their email and BT ID overnight, but managed to request a PIN before whoever was accessing the account could change the telephone number attached to it. That account has not been independently verified, and it isn't clear whether the apparent takeover was connected to the flood of PIN messages. The cause of the wider problem remains a mystery. It isn’t yet clear whether it’s the result of someone deliberately hammering a password recovery mechanism, a fault within BT's systems, or something else entirely. The Register has asked BT how many customers are affected, whether the messages are being generated by external password-reset attempts, and whether it has found any evidence of malicious activity. We've also asked the telco what rate limiting it applies to password reset requests, given reports of hundreds of PINs arriving within minutes, and whether both email and SMS messages are affected. BT says it's investigating. events.title: The public wants a say in AI development
events.summary: Democratic and Republican voters agree that the American public should decide the future of AI development, not billionaires in Silicon Valley, according to new polling shared first with Semafor. The poll was commissioned for a new organization launched by Alex Bores , who made a name for himself as a top target of the AI industry in his failed bid for Congress in New York. Though AI ranked last on a list of 13 issues that 1,502 registered voters polled this month said they care about, half said AI is moving too fast and 86% identified lack of regulation as a problem. Only 18% of those polled think the US falling behind China competitively is a problem, a risk President Donald Trump has cited in opposing regulation. While just 36% polled said they had heard about incidents like the Hugging Face hack, “support for reasonable regulations is actually quite correlated with all these other issues,” Bores told Semafor Tuesday in Washington on the sidelines of the “pro-human” summit attended by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Steve Bannon. The poll’s results, Bores argued, show that “if you show good work on AI, you’re winning over voters, even though AI isn’t their top issue.” Bores’ new organization, Who Decides, aims to help the broader Democratic coalition unite around a “shared baseline” for AI protections. The organization will help traditionally Democratic groups like labor and civil society craft AI policy messages, Bores said. “As a Democrat, I say this with love, but we turn everything into a circular firing squad, and I think it’s really, really important that on this issue, where we have powerful, well-resourced enemies that don’t want there to be any regulation whatsoever, that we are all on the same tea,” he said.

events.title: What is happening to UK prices?
events.summary: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target. The rise was in line with what economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months. Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%. How is the UK's inflation rate measured and what does it mean for UK interest rates? The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026 , while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed. The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation. The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) , external , and the latest figure is published every month. The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%. Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises. But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy. For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals. Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment. Although CPI inflation of 3.1% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. That was the highest rate for 40 years. While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly. The higher figure for August was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 23% compared to August last year. Food price inflation remained at 1.3%. But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran. How do energy prices affect UK inflation? Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine. Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026. But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario. When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July . As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the increase in household energy bills from 1 July when the new Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher. The new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced that VAT on household electricity bills will be scrapped , but that will not take effect until October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation. Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs. Core CPI was 2.6% in the 12 months to August 2026, unchanged from the 12 months to July. Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 days ago What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 26 August What does an Andy Burnham-led government mean for your money? Published 22 July What is happening to UK interest rates and will they fall again? The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023. In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario. At its June meeting, just after a tentative agreement to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, the Bank held interest rates , but oil prices have since risen. The Bank held rates again in July and is expected to do the same in September, but it has indicated it could raise them if the Iran war escalates. Will UK interest rates go up? events.title: Goldman's investment banking chief shares how she uses AI most — and how juniors should use it to get ahead
events.summary: Posnett said junior employees need to strike a balance with their AI usage. Bloomberg/Getty Images Kim Posnett, co-head of investment banking at Goldman, said AI "raises the bar" for client meetings. She said junior bankers need to strike the right balance with AI and offered five pieces of advice. Though AI can automate grunt work, Posnett said learning the technical basics remains important. Even the highest echelons of Goldman Sachs' investment bank are having to re-learn the art of the client meeting. Kim Posnett , the firm's co-head of investment banking, said AI has transformed the nature of those meetings for the bank and the client, both of whom can now access and understand far more information. Now, the CEOs, founders, and investors she talks to have higher expectations for good advice. "It raises the bar for having high-impact meetings, because everyone is more educated and more intelligent before the meeting," she said. Posnett also uses AI to synthesize intel faster when preparing to meet with clients and, in turn, spends time on higher-order thinking, as she said is true for many senior bankers. Kim Posnett is the co-head of investment banking at Goldman Sachs. Goldman Sachs Junior bankers are similarly better prepared to sit in on client meetings, which is accelerating an apprenticeship culture that's central to the firm's identity, Posnett said. The youngest analysts can now spend more time where the true learning lives: listening to complex conversations and watching how senior bankers advise clients through high-stakes choices. Find the right AI balance Goldman Sachs spent around $6 billion on technology , and the bank's CEO, David Solomon, advised this year's interns to experiment with AI in his annual letter . As Posnett sees it, young people across industries should take his advice and aim to "learn faster, to prepare better, and to spend more time on higher-value work." For investment banking analysts at Goldman Sachs, she said that often means speeding up the research process, maybe by summarizing earnings calls or analyzing industry trends. Yet juniors need to find the right balance between mastering AI and depending on it, Posnett said. "Learn how the technology works, experiment with it, use it, and understand how it can make you more productive," she said. "But my second piece of advice is even more important: invest heavily in the human skills that AI struggles to perfectly replicate, ask better questions, develop judgment, learn how to communicate, build relationships, and earn trust. " Posnett recently gave Goldman's incoming analysts and associates five pieces of advice on using AI: master the technical essentials of investment banking, learn to ask better questions, use the time that AI creates wisely, lean into apprenticeship acceleration, and focus on distinctly human qualities that matter in business. Though AI can replace many of the tedious tasks that have historically defined the early years of investment banking — making slide decks and building models, for example — Posnett said it's still important to understand the basics of the job. "There's no substitute for developing technical expertise and judgment, a deep understanding of markets, clients, and businesses," she said. "It doesn't matter if the AI gives you answers if you don't understand what it's saying. You can only build those capabilities through experience and repetition." events.title: Montana Senate candidate who shot a stand-in Flock camera in a campaign ad calls for federal limits on surveillance tech
events.summary: Seth Bodnar, who is running for US Senate in Montana, called for federal regulation on surveillance tech. William Campbell/Getty Images A new campaign ad from Seth Bodnar, an Independent running for US Senate in Montana, targets Flock. Bodnar said he supports federal legislation to address privacy risks posed by Flock. "This isn't an issue that's about left or right," Bodnar said. Seth Bodnar pulls a shotgun from the back of his truck, lines up his mark on a tree stump with a bag of flour set behind, takes aim, and pulls the trigger. His target? A Flock camera . Or a stand-in for one at least. Bodnar, an Independent running for US Senate in Montana , performed the stunt in a new campaign ad shared this week. The veteran and former University of Montana president told Business Insider that Flock cameras are an issue on which voters across the political spectrum can agree. "This isn't an issue that's about left or right," he said. "This is about individual freedom." Bodnar said he put out the video because Montanans have told him they don't want a corporation logging every trip they take, whether it's to church, the doctor, the gun store, or a friend's house. They're not alone. Flock Safety has drawn the ire of Americans across the country, who have taken issue with the company's automated license-plate readers, which are found in thousands of communities in the US. Trump says he "likes" Flock cameras. I say "Flock off." pic.twitter.com/NekA0w4VJd — Seth Bodnar for Montana (@SethBodnarForMT) September 14, 2026 In addition to privacy concerns, critics have pointed to cases in which the tech has misidentified plates or police have misused the data, like by monitoring an ex. A Business Insider investigation found several cases where police using Flock wrongfully targeted or arrested a person who had not committed a crime. Flock and police departments have said the technology has been helpful in addressing crime, including vehicle break-ins, and finding missing people. Last month, the company rolled out new guardrails , such as reducing the default retention period for data, in response to the backlash. Some local and state jurisdictions have also responded by cutting their use of Flock . Call for federal limits on surveillance tech Bodnar said he supports the bipartisan Flock-Off Act, introduced this month by Reps. Thomas Massie and Eric Burlison, which is intended to cut federal funding used for automated license-plate readers and biometric surveillance cameras. He thinks the federal government should go further, calling the proposed act a "starting point." While he does not want Flock cameras banned, he said there could be national standards for the technology, such as how long data is stored, restrictions on how the data can be used, required audits, and penalties for misuse. He also said rules should be set for how data collected by private cameras, such as those belonging to retailers rather than law enforcement, can be used. "We should also close the private camera loophole so police can't use a retailer's camera to do without a warrant what they shouldn't be able to do," he said. Flock's automated license-plate readers are used by police departments and retail stores across the US. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Bodnar is running to replace retiring Republican Sen. Steve Daines this November. A Montana Free Press-Rutgers Eagleton poll released last week found Republican Kurt Alme had an 8-point lead over Bodnar, with Democratic and Libertarian candidates trailing further behind. His new campaign ad went beyond Flock, noting concerns about tech companies buying and selling Americans' data, as well as the development of data centers. "It's the broader data economy: Big Tech collecting, storing, profiting from information about our lives, that data being stored in the cloud by private companies," he explained, adding that "once it exists, it can be accessed, it can be misused, it can be breached." Despite taking aim in his ad, Bodnar said he does not support vandalizing or destroying Flock cameras, as some opponents of the technology have done, and that the issue should be addressed at the ballot box. As for the camera he shoots in the video? A simple decoy, the kind used to deter crime without actually recording anything. "Respect private property rights. Don't touch cameras that aren't yours," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Household income hits record, but lower earners lose ground
events.summary: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements ; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show. Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs , uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net. The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's " Big Beautiful Bill" took hold. That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next. By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967. Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060. The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people. Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%. State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly. Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains. Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile. The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%. Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025. Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median household income among Hispanics, $73,260, showed no significant change from 2024. Meanwhile, 21.8% of Hispanic adults ages 19 to 64 were uninsured in 2025, down a bit from the previous year — but still the highest uninsured rate among the major racial and ethnic groups shown by Census Yes, but: Big racial income gaps remain even as some groups posted gains. Asian American households had the highest median income at $126,300 in 2025, compared with $91,930 for white households and $59,980 for Black American households. Black Americans' household income rose 4.8% from 2024 and whites' household income rose 3%, while Asian Americans' household income showed no significant change. Zoom out: A broader measure of hardship paints a less rosy picture. The Supplemental Poverty Measure , which factors in taxes, government benefits, housing, work and medical expenses, held statistically steady at 13.1% — nearly 3 percentage points above the government's official poverty rate. Medical expenses put an estimated 7.7 million more people below the supplemental poverty line in 2025, the Census Bureau said. Between the lines: Health insurance coverage held steady overall in 2025. The uninsured rate remained statistically unchanged at 7.9%, or 26.7 million people. Medicaid coverage fell 0.5 percentage points nationally, from 17.6% to 17.1% of the population — representing about 1.4 million fewer people with Medicaid coverage in 2025 than in the previous year Among adults ages 19 to 64, 17.3% had public health coverage — including Medicaid, Medicare and VA/CHAMPVA coverage — down 0.5 percentage points from 2024. Census says the decline was driven by a 0.6-point drop in Medicaid coverage among working-age adults. What we're watching: The 2025 numbers may represent the last snapshot before major federal safety-net cuts begin showing up in the Census data, Robert Greenstein, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution, tells Axios.

events.title: ‘We need to get it right’: union gusto for Burnham will face make-or-break tests
events.summary: TUC conference rings with praise for new No 10 team, but battles loom over workers’ rights and north sea drilling L ouise Haigh, the UK first secretary, got a standing ovation from trade union members in Brighton this week, as she acknowledged what she called “the necessity to be bolder in this second chance that we’ve been allowed”. Haigh was the stand-in at the annual TUC congress for Andy Burnham, absent because of his father’s death. The headlines from the seaside gathering were dominated by party funding, after Reform announced £72m of donations in a single weekend and Unite called for a cap on donations by individuals in response. But as they gathered to swap gossip in Brighton’s pubs and hotel bars, senior union figures seemed reinvigorated for the moment by the “Burnham bounce”. Relations between the new No 10 team and the unions – including those less than popular with Keir Starmer’s regime – have improved significantly; general secretaries speak warmly of recent chats with “Andy”. Yet there is a clear sense that the real tests are to come – on the implementation of improved workers’ rights; on oil and gas licences, of particular concern to Unite and the GMB; and on John Healey’s crucial autumn budget. TUC delegates voted through policy statements on a slew of tricky issues in Burnham’s prime ministerial in-tray, from the future relationship with the EU – unions want him to drop Labour’s “red lines” – to Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms . And senior union figures were keen to point to issues they see as make-or-break. Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said she was pleased to see her former schoolmate Jonathan Reynolds back in cabinet as business secretary – but would judge him by results. In particular, she hopes to see the provisions in the Employment Rights Act on abolishing zero-hours contracts implemented in a way that embraces all workers in the retail and hospitality sectors she represents. “A lot of people think, job done – but the implementation means everything,” she said. “For this to make a real difference to people’s lives, we need to get it right. We want everybody to have a contract that reflects the hours they work.” The TUC is also gearing up to campaign on the issue in the coming weeks and months. “We will be getting our message out loud and clear, to Johnny Reynolds in particular,” she said. “It’s about reducing that one-sided flexibility, which employers have got in abundance.” Thomas also echoed a concern shared by several other senior union figures, about whether Reynolds’s newly expanded Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), would end up lacking focus. “I would like to see a minister for work. BIST has so much to do, I worry that the labour stuff gets lost,” she warned. Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, whose members include scientists and engineers – and which is not affiliated to Labour – expresses a similar concern, from a different perspective. Prospect is campaigning against real-terms cuts to science budgets by the taxpayer-backed UK Research and Innovation agency. Clancy frets that folding science into the department may lead to it being seen primarily through a business lens. “This is the first test of BIST … and whether this department’s really going to understand science culture,” he said. The GMB and Unite are waiting anxiously for the government’s ruling on the controversial question of whether to allow drilling in the Jackdaw gas and Rosebank oilfields. A decision had previously been expected this week, but appears to have been postponed until after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in early October, in which the Green party’s leader in England, Zack Polanski, is standing. The two unions’ leaders are such ardent champions of continuing to exploit the North Sea’s declining fields, that Unite’s Sharon Graham and the GMB’s Gary Smith raised concerns about the idea that former energy secretary Ed Miliband would be Burnham’s chancellor. “What that gives us is time,” Graham said of the idea of exploiting Jackdaw and Rosebank. “It gives time for someone to get their backside into gear and realise we have to create an industry over the other side of this, whether it’s green fuel, whether it’s something else. All of that has to be done before you start saying you’re going to choke off what’s going on over here.” But the apparent delay until after a tricky London byelection underlines the fact that other parts of Labour’s electoral coalition are unlikely to welcome a “yes” to future drilling. Meanwhile Graham, who was an outspoken critic of Starmer, said she hoped the first Burnham budget would contain what she characterises as “winter fuel in reverse”. Rachel Reeves’s early decision to severely limit winter fuel payments to pensioners – eventually reversed – came to symbolise the last government’s missteps. “The abhorrence of that: do something as good as that,” Graham said.

events.title: ‘Pacing’ won’t eliminate the risk of AI doom. Here’s what could | David Krueger
events.summary: ‘Pacing’ won’t eliminate the risk of AI doom. Here’s what could The stark reality is this: we don’t know how to maintain control of these systems. But there are actions we can take W ith Jacob Coxon’s resignation from Anthropic , we have reached the AI risk tipping point. Millions of people are finally coming to understand what experts have known for years: AI companies have been gambling with all of our lives, and the odds are not good. In response, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has introduced a proposal for “pacing the frontier”, endorsed by Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Can we breathe a sigh of relief? Are we about to step back from the edge of extinction? Amodei envisions a slowdown of one to two years, resulting in “profound progress” on technical safety measures. But that’s not what humanity needs right now. What we need is a plan in which we’re confident AI isn’t going to kill us, and this isn’t it. The stark reality is this: we don’t know how these AI systems work. We don’t know how to prevent them from misbehaving. We don’t know how to stay in control once they’re smarter than us. We don’t know how to make sure they’re not playing nice or playing dumb to trick our safety tests. We can’t count on solving these problems with another one or two years of research. I know because I have been researching such problems for more than a decade, including as an AI professor at both the University of Cambridge and the University of Montreal. If we want to reduce the risks from AI to an acceptable level, what we actually need is an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development. Is this really possible? It’s a legitimate question, and geopolitics is the crux: how can countries such as the US and China verify each others’ compliance? Donald Trump recently slammed AI regulation , citing the US’s lead in the AI arms race against Beijing. But a simple solution is available: de-commission the advanced computer chips necessary to build these AI models. The massive – and already massively unpopular – datacenter build-out could be reversed. The US and China could take turns decommissioning data centers and the chips they contain. If all parties knew that nobody had the means of building more powerful AI, verification would be simple. To make such an arrangement durable, we could additionally dismantle the supply chain for producing advanced AI chips, which is extremely concentrated and relies on some of the most advanced technology in the world: extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography. Any attempt to operate a covert lithography operation at the scale required for frontier AI development would almost certainly be noticed by other nations’ intelligence services. This plan has benefits over alternative approaches that rely on restricting how computer chips are used. Amodei calls pausing “unlikely”, but an agreement to decommission AI infrastructure would actually be easier to verify than Amodei’s proposals for global coordination, which would require increasing levels of surveillance as computing hardware continues to advance and proliferate. The economic costs of this plan would be substantial, but given the stakes, unless we have a better plan that actually saves our lives, they are clearly worth it. During the Covid-19 pandemic, governments shut down significant parts of society and the economy to save lives. We should be willing to go to much greater lengths to prevent the extinction of our species. I’m actively researching “softer” versions of the proposal that would involve creating computer chips that can be used to run AI models, but not to build more powerful ones. And other researchers have also developed proposals for an indefinite moratorium. Amodei’s essay, sadly, does not consider these pause proposals. His plan is ultimately still to have AIs build smarter and smarter AIs with less human involvement – “recursive self-improvement”, a project designed to render humans obsolete. What should we actually expect to come of Amodei’s plan? Step one would “embed” external evaluators from organizations such as METR , which was invited to investigate the OpenAI-Hugging Face scandal. Big tech CEOs may call this “radical”, but let’s be clear: what they’re actually talking about is more self-regulation. Three years ago, I helped found the UK AI Security Institute – another leading evaluator. I quit after it was clear the ecosystem was getting the burden of proof formula backwards. Today, AI is still de facto “safe-until-proven dangerous”. The safety standards Amodei suggests are guaranteed to fall far short of those in other safety-critical industries like aviation. We simply don’t know how to do recursive self-improvement safely. So let’s stop. Let’s stop making AI we can’t control, and let’s stop listening to the AI industry about how it wants to be regulated. Proposals for a pause are being put forth in both the US and UK legislatures.

events.title: Big-money donations poison British politics. We can stop the mega-rich buying access and influence | Gordon Brown
events.summary: Big-money donations poison British politics. We can stop the mega-rich buying access and influence I’ve seen how imbalances in campaign spending can distort democracy. The multimillion-pound gifts to Reform must act as a final wake-up call T he British people cannot be bought, but their views and votes can be heavily influenced by a flood of political party propaganda – from expensive advertising and constant leaflet drops to personalised online messages targeted directly at voters. When I fought the election of 2010, there was a massive imbalance in spending. In 2007 we had inherited Labour party debts of £25m following the 2005 election – and with such tight finances Labour was able to spend only £8m in 2010 , in contrast to the Conservatives’ £17m. We lost out in particular by being unable to invest in the new forms of online advertising coming on stream. But the imbalances are likely to become even starker in future as the recent donations to Reform show. A decade ago, only 1% of individuals and companies making political donations gave of the order of £1m or more. By 2024, they accounted for over a third , at 35%. These latest record-breaking donations from crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne are worth more than all donations to UK political parties in 2025 combined. Spending more money at an election almost certainly leads to greater electoral success . This is worrying – and while the government recently tasked the Electoral Commission with reviewing campaign spending limits , more must be done. The reforms to election financing recommended by the Commission on the UK’s Future, which I chaired, and in particular a donation cap, should be introduced into the representation of the people bill now in the House of Lords . Nearly half of voters , with few objecting, say they would view a party more favourably if it introduced a limit on political donations. Indeed, the very fact that money has been openly solicited in return for political access and, potentially, influence – as well as positions of public office and honours – exposes our democracy and weakens public trust. A cap on individual donations was recommended by the independent Hayden Phillips review in 2007, by the Committee on Standards in Public Life in 2011 – and by an increasing number of senior politicians, including John Major . Indeed, in December 2025, the UK and at least 59 other countries co-sponsored a United Nations resolution that urges state parties to consider “limitations on donations … with a view to combating corruption”. Other comparable democracies impose donation caps. Canada caps donations to political parties at about £930 annually; France caps donations to political parties at £6,400 annually and £3,900 for presidential campaigns; Italy’s cap is £85,600 per person or company annually. “My gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k,” Andy Burnham said just before he became prime minister, and in September Stella Creasy and 63 other MPs backed an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which was then withdrawn, to introduce an annual donation cap of £500,000, decreasing to £100,000 after one calendar year. The new bill should include an enabling power for the secretary of state to set a cap on donations, having consulted the Ethics and Integrity Commission (formerly the Committee on Standards in Public Life) as well as the Electoral Commission. Some want this cap to include donations by trade unions. But a collection of individual members who provide small contributions and can opt out do not pose the same level of risk to our democracy as multimillion-pound donations from private donors. Outside general election years, Labour and Conservative party spending has recently been around £60m and £55m , respectively. Transparency International UK has calculated that before 2024, the total spend in election years was about £74m and £87m. In 2024, it says that Labour expenditure ballooned to a record-breaking £103m while the Conservative party spent less – just £74m. But paradoxically, this imbalance was made possible by the Conservative government’s decision to raise general election spending limits . Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Donors to the Labour party whom I have met favour a cap on donations; in fact, they say their recent larger-than-normal donations were made simply to even up the odds between political parties. How would things change? Transparency International UK has made a tool to model the potential impact of donation caps on political party finances. Setting a donation cap of £50,000 per year, you can see the impact of reducing big-money donations. At the same time, there would still be sufficient funding for political parties to campaign effectively and fairly, without a need for additional public funds. It is now time to create such a level playing field.

events.title: Company behind failed Surrey oilfield project sells site at massive loss
events.summary: New owners apply for permission to extract oil in Horse Hill despite landmark ruling from supreme court in 2024 After years of trying to dig for oil in Surrey , the company behind the drilling project that was turned down in a landmark supreme court ruling has sold off the site for a fraction of the money it spent on it, and rebranded as a clean energy company. Meanwhile, the new owners, who picked up the site for £1m, are applying, once again, for permission to dig. UK Oil and Gas (UKOG) spent more than a decade trying to develop Horse Hill oilfields, where they said they had found 100bn barrels of oil . But in 2024 the supreme court, in a decision which has since become known as the Finch Ruling , decreed that “a planning authority should have considered the indirect downstream greenhouse gas emissions of an oil and gas project as part of its environmental impact assessment” and overturned a council decision to let expansion go ahead. The Guardian understands that the implied value of the Horse Hill licence area reached a peak of £46m in September 2018 after UKOG agreed to buy a 14.3% economic stake from a group of vendors for £6.6m. The surging valuations given to the fields was driven by industry estimates that there could be about 9.24bn barrels of oil in the tight Jurassic shale and conventional reservoir sections within the Horse Hill licences. Public records appear to show UKOG invested more than £25m into the site. Prior to the £1m sale, UKOG’s financial accounts showed that it had written down the value of its Horse Hill interests to just £55,360 on its balance sheet. UKOG has now changed its name to UK Energy Group, seeking to shift its focus towards salt-cavern energy storage and other clean energy projects. Stephen Sanderson, the company’s chief executive, said while the company still sees “potentially material resources” at Horse Hill, the divestment presented “timely and attractive opportunity to complete UKOG’s exit from the UK onshore oil and gas sector”. The company reportedly raised £1m in 2025 to develop hydrogen-storage projects in south Dorset and Yorkshire, and a further £500,000 to acquire land for a proposed East Yorkshire salt-cavern site. Guy Prince, the head of energy supply at energy transition thinktank Carbon Tracker, said Horse Hill was an example of “regulatory stranding”, in which climate litigation and regulatory shifts undermine the value of a fossil fuel asset. “The same transition risk can have really radical financial consequences depending on who owns the asset,” he said. “For a major [company], it might impair one investment opportunity. But for a small company concentrated on one project like this, it just transformed the entire business.” New owner Energy B is taking over UKOG’s application to drill for oil in Surrey. Horse Hill Developments Ltd, which it now controls, submitted a renewed planning application to Surrey county council in May for four production wells, a new oil processing area, tanker-loading facilities and a fluid reinjection well. The proposal would allow nearly 700,000 tonnes of oil to be extracted over 20 years. Sarah Finch, the campaigner who brought the successful legal challenge to the supreme court in 2024 , said there were “serious shortcomings” with the application’s new environmental assessment. “New guidance from the government and pre-existing guidance all say that they have to place the emissions from a new proposed project within a cumulative context of all current and approved fossil fuel projects,” Finch said. “They didn’t make any attempt to do that, although the data is readily available out there.” The application estimates that the development would result in about 2.3m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions over its lifetime, including emissions from the eventual burning of the oil, but concluded the impact was “insignificant”. Planning documents said: “Horse Hill would account for around 0.05% of the projected UK carbon budget; an insignificant contribution that would give rise to insignificant climate change effects.” The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Finch said the developer’s argument was “false”. “Any greenhouse gas emissions are significant,” she added. “The International Energy Agency has said we can’t afford any new oil or gas. Any additional fossil fuels are going to make it impossible to stay within the 1.5C target, so [the emissions] are significant.” The application argued that extracting up to 678,693 tonnes of oil at Horse Hill would improve energy security by reducing the UK’s reliance on imports. An Energy B spokesperson said: “At a time of global uncertainty and energy price shocks, domestic oil and gas production increases energy security. “We are confident of meeting all the necessary legal and environmental requirements for the site.

events.title: Tech giants launch flexible-power coalition for data centers
events.summary: A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all. The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure. The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper. What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance . State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE. The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call. The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it. Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday . More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago. In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them. How it works: Data centers have traditionally been treated as giant, round-the-clock power users. The coalition wants to change the rules so facilities that can reliably cut their grid demand when electricity supplies are tight can get connected faster and potentially avoid some costly grid upgrades. The flexibility could come from shifting or pausing AI computing jobs, tapping batteries or nearby power generation, coalition leaders said. Google has committed 1 gigawatt of power demand it can reduce when needed through utility agreements nationwide, said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation. The group plans to push the approach with federal and state regulators, regional grid operators and utilities. Yes, but: The bargain depends on data centers actually delivering the flexibility they promise. Sivaram said facilities should qualify for faster or larger connections only if their ability to cut demand is "verifiable and enforceable." Reality check: Convincing communities that this complicated solution can actually address their concerns will be a tall order. "Power-flexible data centers are a wonky topic," Sivaram told Axios. His pitch: Data centers could cut their electricity use when the grid is stressed, helping avoid costly infrastructure while bringing in revenue that can support other electricity users. The goal, Sivaram said, is to turn data centers into "good grid citizens" that communities see as assets rather than burdens. What we're watching: Whether regulators actually create the fast lane the coalition wants. Federal regulators in June directed regional grid operators to examine new options for connecting large, flexible power users, providing an opening for the approach AEMA is advocating. Editor's note: Amy Harder is a fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth, but was not involved in the polling and received no advance access beyond that provided to other journalists. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that 76% of Republicans (not 78%) support requiring data center developers to pay for grid upgrades.

events.title: Polymarket’s Next Bet? It Can Also Be a Media Company
events.summary: Every day, a newsletter from the prediction market Polymarket hits my inbox with a subject line that could easily come from any number of politics-focused newspapers or magazines. Recent entries include “Houthis Reveal New Precision Strike Capabilities,” “BREAKING: Trump Unveils Green Energy Beam,” and “World War I, 2.0?” These dispatches are roundups with breathless summaries of the day’s top stories, linking out to corresponding Polymarket markets—yes, this thing will happen; no, it won’t. As far as business news analysis goes, the newsletter is not exactly Bloomberg’s Money Stuff , or even Emily Sundberg’s Feed Me —but it’s recognizably a commercial editorial product, and one that plays an important role in the prediction market ecosystem. The industry is currently embroiled in a series of legal battles over whether prediction markets are financial services (the view held by the markets and the federal government) or gambling platforms (the position of many state authorities and regulators). The fight over what kind of companies these are could end up in the Supreme Court, but in the meantime, both Polymarket and its even-more-popular archrival, Kalshi, have successfully positioned themselves as new media organizations too. For two companies associated with risk, it’s a notably old-school hedge. All kinds of tech startups have launched editorial projects—did you know the alternative dating app Feeld has a surprisingly good magazine?—but the leading prediction markets are entrenching themselves into the mainstream media apparatus in a particularly aggressive way. A recent report noted that they’re integrated into a quarter of the top 20 companies listed in the S&P 500’s Communications Services sector. Polymarket has partnerships with Dow Jones and Substack, while Kalshi has deals with CNN, CNBC, and Fox Corp. None of the agreements facilitate trading. Instead, they’re mainly about data sharing; news outlets want to know what people are putting their money on, and prediction markets are happy to oblige. The deals showcase prediction markets as information channels—places to go to find out about what’s happening. They’ve given Polymarket and Kalshi much-needed boosts in credibility and offered a straightforward introduction to the wider public. Prediction market boosters hype these products as “truth machines,” revealing public sentiment more accurately than polling or traditional reporting; when media outlets decide the odds themselves are newsworthy , they reinforce that message. “Given the forecasting success of the markets, it's clear there is informational value,” says Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such. “And three out of four users don't trade, which suggests the informational use case is popular enough to be taken very seriously.” (Polymarket declined to comment.) Providing data is only a small part of how these companies function as new media entities. On social media, their official accounts post like news outlets, adopting a vernacular that mashes up PopCrave’s frenzied sensibility with Bloomberg’s coverage areas. (The efforts haven’t been wholly reliable: A New York Times analysis earlier this year found that Polymarket’s newsy social accounts have published “false and misleading information.”) Chief executive and founder Shayne Coplan has referred to the company’s partnership with X as “News 2.0.” In 2024, the company hinted at even more expansive ambitions, recruiting for an editor in chief role to lead “content and data journalism” efforts. It never made that hire, although political analyst and media founder Nate Silver came on later that year as an adviser. But on its careers page , the company beckons prospective employees by playing this angle up: “Become the new front page of the internet.” Kalshi is less inclined to describe itself this way. When asked if it considered itself a media company, Such, the spokesperson, tells WIRED that it does not, though the markets themselves have “quasi-media” attributes because they follow the news. “We see ourselves as a financial exchange,” he says. Sure. But why not both? Financial services companies have jumped into the media sector before, most obviously Bloomberg, which initially focused on providing market data and financial analytics before expanding to include journalism products. More recently, the online trading hub Robinhood—now also a Polymarket competitor with its own prediction market offerings—ran a media subsidiary called Sherwood before winding it down earlier this summer. Then there’s Hunterbook, which operates both an investigative outlet called Hunterbook News and a hedge fund that executes trades based on its outlet’s investigations. Polymarket doesn’t have a dedicated subsidiary or editorial arm. But it has launched a weekly podcast called What Are the Odds? in partnership with the podcast network Dear Media.

events.title: Arizona Made Its English Fluency Test Easier to Pass. Experts Say It Will Harm Students’ Ability to Succeed.
events.summary: Samantha Ramos teaches students in her English language development class at John B. Wright Elementary School in Tucson, Arizona. Cassidy Araiza for ProPublica Samantha Ramos stood at the front of her second grade classroom, a small mic clipped to her lanyard amplifying her instructions as she began a phonics lesson. “Can we get our arms ready?” asked Ramos, who’s taught at the John B. Wright Elementary School in Tucson, Arizona, for 15 years. She brought her right palm to her left shoulder as the students imitated her movements. Ramos, who specializes in teaching English as a second language, was leading a lesson that day on the short “i” sound. She told the students to pronounce each letter with a different gesture — touching the shoulder for the “w,” the elbow for the “i” and the hand for the double “l” — before sounding out the word “will.” They repeated the process for other short “i” words — “dig,” “wig” and “fit.” The lesson is part of a daily block of language instruction, ranging from two to four hours long, that Arizona students learning English as a second language are required to take. The students, most of them Spanish-speaking Latino children, remain in the program, separated for part of that time from their peers whose primary language is English, until they pass a test showing they’re fluent enough to learn in a mainstream classroom. The program is known as “structured English immersion,” or colloquially as “English-only” because all instruction is required to be in English. This limits their time for core subjects, like math and science, that are critical to academic success and college readiness. Arizona is the only state with English-only laws still in effect for its public schools. But the number of students enrolled in the curriculum has tumbled dramatically this year. At the Tucson Unified School District, where Ramos teaches, the percentage of test-taking students who scored high enough to be classified as proficient in English more than doubled — from 10% in 2025 to 24% in 2026. Rather than a big leap in fluency, however, the test results reflect the Arizona Department of Education lowering the grade needed to pass. The changes were approved by outgoing Superintendent of Public Instruction Tom Horne, a longtime Republican defender of Arizona’s English-only policies. Experts warn this change will do lasting harm to tens of thousands of Arizona students who will exit the structured English immersion program before they know the language well enough to succeed. Such students are already part of the lowest-performing group on standardized tests, and the loss of specialized instruction could further harm their long-term academic success, according to education researchers. Past attempts by the Arizona Department of Education to reclassify large numbers of children learning English as fluent prompted federal investigations by the departments of Justice and Education. Federal officials contended placing such students in classrooms where they struggled because they lacked knowledge of English violated their civil and educational rights, and Arizona agreed to a settlement more than a decade ago. What’s happening now could be a repeat of that, said Katie Bernstein, an applied linguist and professor of early childhood education at Arizona State University. “If you’re put in a class where you don’t understand what’s going on at all, you’re not learning language or content,” she said. “And so those are the worst outcomes of all, are students who are not given any language services.” Ramos teaches her students phonics during a daily block of English-language immersion. Cassidy Araiza for ProPublica Nearly 1 in 10 students enrolled in Arizona public and charter schools marked in their school registration forms they speak a language other than English at home. State law mandates that they be assessed for fluency and placed in structured English immersion, and each spring they take the Arizona English Language Learner Assessment, or AZELLA, to measure their progress in reading, writing, speaking and listening. This approach has been required since Arizona voters passed a 2000 ballot initiative, Proposition 203, banning bilingual education in public schools. Still, officials have periodically made changes to the proficiency test. The U.S. departments of Justice and Education determined the version of AZELLA administered between 2006 and 2012 — coinciding with Horne’s first two terms as the state’s top education official — was “not a valid measure of English language proficiency and readiness.” As a result, the state had removed at least 28,000 students from structured English immersion who still lacked proficiency in reading and writing the language. The Arizona Department of Education was found to be in violation of civil rights laws that ban discrimination on the basis of race and national origin by schools that receive federal funds. The state voluntarily entered a settlement , which stressed that the law requires “education agencies to take appropriate action to overcome language barriers that impede students’ equal participation in instructional programs.” Do You Have Experience With Arizona’s Structured English Immersion System, Also Called English-Only? Have stories to tell about how Arizona treats children learning English in public schools? Share your tips with Rafael Carranza at englishlearners@azluminaria.org . The settlement agreement stipulated that the state would immediately help school districts find the students who had been harmed and offer “reading and writing intervention services.” In the long term, the state was required to revamp the AZELLA test. Similar issues prompted a second voluntary settlement four years later , which instructed the state to raise the threshold for a test score to qualify as proficient in English. The state was also required to retest English-language learners using more rigorous standards, among other things. Ida Rose Florez, a psychologist and former professor and researcher at Arizona State University, conducted a study published in 2012 that found the AZELLA test was “ineffective and obsolete” and its results could be arbitrary. The research concluded there was no evidence the test could “accurately differentiate” between children who need English-language services and those who don’t. “What I examined, and what I saw, was a test that was absolutely not developed correctly,” Florez told Arizona Luminaria and ProPublica. “I don’t see any basis for validity whatsoever.” After dropping during the pandemic, AZELLA passing rates held steady at 12% statewide for three school years, including in 2025, when more than 118,000 took the test and just over 14,000 scored well enough to be reclassified as proficient. events.title: Justice threatens GOP showdown in West Virginia
events.summary: The News Jim Justice is getting the itch. And it could set up a battle of GOP titans. The West Virginia GOP senator is considering a run for his old job as governor in 2028, which would potentially set up a race between him and incumbent Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Justice told Semafor he’s “sure thinking about it” before quickly interjecting that he loves “what I’m doing here” in the Senate. He also jabbed at Morrisey but insisted he wants the governor to be successful: “Gov. Morrisey has a more difficult time bonding with people and everything, but beyond that, I want him to do great, I really do. I’m not in a food fight at all.” “I do love the people of West Virginia, and I spent eight years trying to build it back. Got it really going,” Justice continued. “I just want goodness for West Virginia, but I want goodness for the whole nation too. We’ll make a decision.” Know More West Virginia is a small state that’s also the home of bare-knuckled politics and big personalities. Republicans recruited Justice, a former Democrat, to run against former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-W.Va., in 2024, though Manchin ultimately decided against seeking reelection. Manchin narrowly defeated Morrisey in 2018, but Morrisey mounted a political comeback in 2024 by emerging from a crowded GOP primary and winning the governor’s mansion. A Morrisey ally told Semafor that Justice has myriad vulnerabilities and hasn’t had to win a tough GOP primary against someone like the incumbent governor (though Justice did easily defeat former Rep. Alex Mooney, R-W.Va., in 2024). The ally added that the conservative Club for Growth is already committed to opposing Justice, put Morrisey’s war chest at nearly $5 million across several political entities, and noted that Justice is in debt and is now sharing control of his family’s Greenbrier resort. But Justice said people in West Virginia are encouraging him to run: “You’re going to hear people come to you and say, ‘Boy, we’d love to have you back as governor.’ You know, that’s natural and everything. I don’t pay a whole lot of attention.” Manchin also flirted repeatedly with running for his old job as governor, which he used to call the “best job in the world.” Manchin never ran after serving in the Senate, but Senate Republicans believe Justice is more likely to run than not, according to several GOP sources. Regarding the 2028 governor race, Manchin said on Tuesday: “Can’t we get through this election before worrying about the next election?”
