events.title: US stocks close lower as oil spikes and the benchmark Treasury yield breaches 5%
events.summary: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange on Sept 15 in New York City. NEW YORK - Wall Street extended its selloff on Sept 15, as rising US Treasury yields, mounting debt concerns and soaring crude prices kept buyers on the sidelines. All three major US stock indexes extended Sept 14’s losses as broad risk-off sentiment weighed on nearly every sector but energy. That sector benefited from expanding hostilities in the Middle East , which included new attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure. “Given rising prices for fuel, especially diesel, given the near-certain outlook for rising rates beginning tomorrow, and given the concerns over the potential slowdown in the AI ecosphere, why step into the market aggressively until some of this clears up?” said Peter Tuz, president of Chase Investment Counsel in Charlottesville, Virginia. The Federal Reserve has convened for its two-day monetary policy meeting, which is due to culminate on Sept 16 with the central bank’s rate decision. With recent economic data showing the labour market on solid footing, while war-related energy price pressures are morphing into broader, systemic inflation, the central bank is expected to implement a 25-basis-point increase to its Fed funds target rate – its first interest rate hike in over three years. In the wake of last week’s hot inflation data and the near 25 per cent jump in US crude prices over the last two weeks, financial markets have priced in a 94.5 per cent likelihood of a rate hike on Sept 16 , up from 33.1 per cent one month ago, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. Tuz added that while markets will learn the Fed’s decision tomorrow, “the Middle East conflict is a wild card as to how long it might last.” Front-month West Texas Intermediate and Brent oil settled up 4.4 per cent and 2.9 per cent respectively, while diesel futures closed at a record high. “This will probably be not a one-and-done, but a series of rate increases,” said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest in Elmhurst, Illinois. “It will be dependent on oil; that is really the source of inflation and it’s starting to seep into other parts of the market.” As rate-hike bets increased, global bond yields resumed their upward climb, with benchmark US Treasury yields breaching 5 per cent and reaching the highest level since 2007. Rising interest rates are increasing the pressure on heavily indebted borrowers, including companies that have placed big bets on AI. Those worries exacerbated mounting fears over AI’s destructive potential and growing opposition to the construction of data centres, which came to a head on Monday and dragged the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index down. The semiconductor index, which has helped drive broader stock market gains this year, did not meaningfully recover from Monday’s rout, eking out a 0.4 per cent gain. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 328.09 points, or 0.63 per cent, to 52,093.11, the S&P 500 lost 34.25 points, or 0.45 per cent, to 7,585.73 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 204.84 points, or 0.78 per cent, to 25,981.57. Among the 11 major sectors of the S&P 500, consumer discretionary stocks were the biggest percentage losers, while energy, buoyed by rising crude, advanced 2.3 per cent. Dave & Buster’s tumbled 19 per cent following the company’s second-quarter revenue miss. Waystar rose 7.1 per cent after Reuters reported the healthcare software firm is exploring options, including a potential sale. events.title: Your AI agents' reports and questions have a new inbox, courtesy of AWS
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Pizza Bot runs locally and lets users interact with AI agents in an email-like interface. Perfect for blowing them off just like your human colleagues! AWS says wartime damage means some Middle East cloud resources are gone for good 1 hour ago TypeSafe AI debuts model for machines that plays Doom 12 hours ago Give Xfce a Mac or Unity-style makeover 1 day ago Open weights are not open source: Why AI's favorite label is under dispute 1 day ago Microsoft drafts feel-good AI model guidelines and wants your input 1 day ago AWS engineers have published an open-source AI agent management tool that treats tasks and permission requests just like emails that fill up an inbox. Pizza Bot was announced on AWS’ open-source blog last week, where it was billed by its developers as a way to more easily manage agent tasks without constantly having to check a chat window to see if a task was completed or on hold because more permission was needed. “You don’t send an email and then sit watching the outbox until the reply lands,” the Pizza Bot team wrote. “Pizza Bot is shaped like an email client for the same reason: a thread is a unit of work you come back to rather than a session you have to attend.” Like the modern email services it mimics, Pizza Bot organizes communications with AI agents into message threads. Finished tasks, along with detailed result writeups you’d expect from a colleague you’ve delegated your work to, end up in the Unread category, while anything you need to make a decision on is shunted to the Action category. Asynchronous agent communication is likely to be a godsend for those balancing multiple tasks assigned to digital delegees, as the Pizza Bot team describes it. “Live chat assumes both parties are present, which holds for a quick exchange and breaks the moment a task takes several minutes,” the Pizza Bot maintainers wrote. Just like you don’t want to stare over the shoulder of the poor IT sod you sent off to do a task while you watch YouTube videos, no one wants to sit there and watch an AI agent do web research, or whatever. “Pizza Bot treats an agent the way you’d treat a colleague who has gone off to do the work: it comes back when there’s something to read, or something only you can decide,” the PB team added. Pizza Bot, named for Amazon’s “ two-pizza team ” model (i.e., small, autonomous teams small enough to be fed by two pizzas), began life inside Amazon as an internal tool for AI agent uses other than software development. According to its developers, non-coding uses they were exploring internally continually had the same requirements, namely working in the background autonomously and only bugging their user when they were done or had a question. “None of those describe how anyone uses a chat window,” the Pizza Bot team explained. “They describe how people already work with each other.” Email, they added, was the perfect design paradigm for internal use, and seeing whether it would work for everyone else meant opening the project to open source contributions. As mentioned, Pizza Bot is open source - you can snag a copy for Windows, macOS, and Linux from its GitHub repo . It runs on-device, stores all its communication threads locally in SQLite files, and doesn’t transmit anything off device unless you grant permission for it to do so. Prompts and attachments are sent to model providers, naturally, but even that’s not necessary: Pizza Bot also supports Ollama, allowing users to run compatible open-weight AI models locally. Pizza Bot doesn’t ship with a lot of capabilities, as its maintainers noted that Amazon-specific skills and MCP servers were left out when they rebuilt it as an open source project for public release. Out of the box, however, it can list, read, write, edit, and search files, delegate tasks to specialist agents, and run a sandboxed JavaScript interpreter. It also ships with a browser automation skill and a guide skill that lets users ask about Pizza Bot’s capabilities.

events.title: Australian company Sharon AI buys former Visy paper mill site at Ettamogah
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ettamogah land sale to AI company raises health and environmental protection concerns The Visy paper mill in Ettamogah has been sold to AI computing company Sharon AI. ( ABC News: Philippe Perez ) Australian-owned AI company Sharon AI has purchased the former Visy paper mill site at Ettamogah. Albury residents have raised concerns about the sale. The company is yet to disclose what it plans to do with the site, but says it will undertake appropriate community consultation. Albury residents have raised concerns about a major industrial site being sold to a company specialising in artificial intelligence (AI). Sharon AI, based in Sydney and New York, has confirmed it has bought the former Visy paper mill site at Ettamogah, north of Albury. The Australian-owned company describes itself as a high-operating computing company "neo-cloud" that rents out its infrastructure and equipment for AI use. The site was sold by Visy to Sharon AI. ( ABC News: Philippe Perez ) "We will say more at a later date." The company would not disclose what it intends to develop at the site, but said it would undertake appropriate community consultation. "Sharon AI is committed to building real-world infrastructure throughout Australia, which creates jobs and a positive impact to local communities," the spokesperson said. Katie Lucantonio lives near the Ettamogah site and said she was concerned about the uncertainty of a potential data centre in the area. "The way I look at it … it's like if Coca-Cola were to purchase it, I would expect there to be some sort of [soft-drink] manufacturing there," Ms Lucantonio said. "Health is the number one [concern]. "Second to that is the environment, and the health of the flora [and] fauna. "It's surrounded by native bushland … and further on, you've got farms nearby. Local resident Katie Lucantonio says her top concern about the paper mill site sale is the community's health. ( Supplied: Katie Lucantonio ) "What I've seen … is if you don't get on the front foot of these issues, particularly in pre-planning stages, there's no, or very little, community consultation." NSW Liberal Albury MP Justin Clancy said the local community had a right to ask questions if a large-scale data centre development was planned. "There are two aspects to this that we need to look at," Mr Clancy said. "Obviously one is we know that our use of data and AI is increasing significantly at a rapid rate in this nation and right across the globe, and there's certainly a call there to make sure that we as a nation have sovereign capability. Earlier this year, the NSW government announced measures to encourage data centre builders to follow new guidelines to fast-track projects. If builders met environmental and efficiency standards and avoided net costs to consumers, the government promised to evaluate applications within 75 days. Proposed legislation for the program is set to be debated in parliament later this year. Justin Clancy says it is right for the community to ask questions about data centre development in regional towns. ( ABC Goulburn Murray: Sarah Krieg ) Albury Mayor Kevin Mack said he could not comment on private land ownership, but any development would be assessed through normal planning processes. "Albury is open for business, and we welcome investment that creates jobs and supports our growing regional economy," Cr Mack said. "Our role is to ensure the right planning and infrastructure are in place so opportunities can be realised when they arise." The Australian Energy Market Operator said about 3 per cent of Australia's electricity was consumed by data centres this past financial year, a figure set to increase to 13 per cent by 2035. Johanna Lim from the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre said the substantial resources needed to operate data centres were cause for community concern. "While the services that these data centres are providing are usually at a national or even global level, many of these impacts tend to be felt more locally, and I think that's a key driver of this debate," she said. Albury is already home to the Leading Edge Data Centre, near the airport. ( ABC News: Philippe Perez ) "Regional areas that have lots of land can provide for these larger sites, and that can be easier to accommodate compared to more land-constrained areas like Sydney and Melbourne." She said more community pushback will change how data centre companies conduct themselves through the planning process.

events.title: Housing market 'normalising' as national resale profits drop
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts National resale profits down but Brisbane still top with $525k median gain Nationally, sellers made a median $371,000, with 95.4 per cent of the 94,000 resales analysed by Cotality returning a profit. ( ABC News: Liz Pickering ) The latest sales figures from Cotality show Brisbane properties made a median of $525,000 profit at resale in the June quarter. Brisbane is the most profitable capital for sellers, despite a national downturn in property prices. Cotality's head of research Gerard Burg said lower prices are likely to "persist for some time". Brisbane is still the country's most profitable capital for sellers despite the housing downturn, while one in five Melbourne units recorded a loss, according to the latest figures from data property firm Cotality. The June quarter data marks the end of record resales, after a 21-year high in March. Brisbane resales had a median profit of $525,000, with 99.8 per cent of sales in the quarter making a gain. Meanwhile in Melbourne, 20.8 per cent of units were sold at a loss, and about one in 10 Sydney units went for less than their purchase price. Houses returned a profit more reliably than units overall, with 97.8 per cent of houses making a gain compared to 90.5 per cent of units. Nationally, sellers made a median $371,000, with 95.4 per cent of the more than 94,000 resales analysed returning a profit. In Sydney, 11.4 per cent of units sold for less than their purchase price. ( ABC: John Gunn ) Head of research at Cotality Gerard Burg said profitability was still "exceptionally high by historical standards" even as a softening housing market pushed down prices. "Most sellers are still benefiting from the significant value growth accumulated over the past five years, which is providing considerable protection against the early stages of the downturn," he said. "With home values falling across more markets, that buffer will become increasingly important in determining resale outcomes." Gerard Burg says the profitability seen in Brisbane contrasted with the weaker performance in Melbourne. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) Mr Burg said there was a "real contrast" in the unit markets, with a "much weaker performance" in Melbourne, where CBD unit values peaked in 2017. "So, it's very hard to get a profitable resale in that type of environment," he said. "In contrast, there's been a lot of demand for units in Brisbane." Brisbane real estate agent Brett Andreassen said the data confirmed what he had been seeing for months — prices have come down. "I think because this crazy growth happened over five years, everyone thought that was the normal — when it really wasn't." Mr Andreassen said sellers whose property had been on the market for months "have still got those previous figures in their heads". "Whereas a lot of the owners that are coming on the market now have adjusted their expectations to the current reality," he said. Brisbane real estate agent Brett Andreassen says the drop in resale profits "definitely rings true". ( Supplied ) Adelaide was the country's second most profitable capital, followed by Perth, with median gains of $472,000 and $470,000, respectively. Home prices in each city had jumped since COVID-19, when relative affordability had boosted interstate migration, Mr Burg said. Meanwhile, regional markets had higher profitable resales than the capitals, with 97.5 per cent compared to 94.1 per cent. Metro sellers still made a bigger gain, with a $415,000 median compared to $324,500. Homes sold in Brisbane last quarter made a median profit of $525,000. ( ABC News: Charlie Mclean ) Mr Burg said the downturn put more recent buyers at risk, with homes held for less time more likely to be resold at a loss. Nationally, the median time between purchase and sale of a house for a profitable resale was typically 9.3 years. The median time off the market for a loss-making house was 4.4 years. How a housing downturn affects your city New Cotality modelling data shows what property prices could look like across the capitals if the market falls by 5, 10, 15 or 20 per cent. "The longer that you hold the property, the less exposed you are to the fluctuations that occur in an individual housing cycle," he said. Mr Burg said the trend of declining values was likely to "persist for some time", which could make a profitable sale becoming "more challenging". "There is significant uncertainty around the short-term economic outlook, particularly the direction of interest rates and increasing pressure on household budgets," he said.

events.title: Meta now lets AI agents handle the boring parts of WhatsApp Business setup
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Alongside news of its new AI-focused subscription plans , Meta announced on Tuesday that it will now allow AI agents of your choosing to set up and manage WhatsApp Business messaging, the service that allows companies to connect with customers through WhatsApp conversations. As Meta explains, this process was previously a bit more cumbersome, as it required developers to move between different tools and services, including the Developer Console, Meta’s Business Manager, the API reference, and their editor. Now, they can instead ask their preferred AI agent to set up WhatsApp Business messaging by chatting with it and describing what needs to be done. This is made possible by the new WhatsApp Business Tools MCP, an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that directly connects an AI coding agent like Claude, Cursor, Codex, or ChatGPT to the WhatsApp Business Platform. The move sees Meta expanding its existing lineup of MCP servers beyond those for managing ads and monitoring app configurations, and other social technologies to one specifically designed to help onboard businesses to WhatsApp. Many other tech companies also offer MCP servers that allow AI agents to securely interact with their services, including PayPal, Stripe, GitHub, Notion, Slack, Salesforce, Atlassian, X , Google , Microsoft , and others. In Meta’s case, the AI agent will handle much of the busywork involved in the WhatsApp Business setup process, like creating the company’s WhatsApp Business account, adding and verifying its phone number, registering it for access to the Cloud API, checking the business’ Terms of Service, and more. Businesses will also be able to use the AI agent for other tasks, like describing a messaging template they want the AI to create or having the agent edit an existing template. Plus, they can test messages and webhooks and monitor things that may previously have quietly failed, like the Terms of Service, payment method, and Business Verification. During setup and configuration, Meta’s other MCP server, Meta Social Technologies MCP, can also be used to discover API endpoints, search documentation, and help troubleshoot errors, the company noted. events.title: Why Australia's most attractive renewables state is almost $1b behind
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NSW's renewable energy rollout is running almost $1b under budget In 2020, the NSW Coalition government outlined a plan for a once-in-a-generation undertaking. To power Australia's most populous state with renewable energy instead of coal, regional areas would be transformed into power stations. Renewable energy zones (REZs) would cluster solar, wind farms and batteries around shared transmission lines. But almost six years on, delivering the infrastructure is taking longer than planned and the state is racing to meet its own targets. The agency responsible for the rollout, EnergyCo, has spent almost $1 billion less than budgeted over the past two years. Ty Christopher, who spent decades delivering grid infrastructure in NSW for the previous state-owned energy corporation, Integral Energy, said there was no "single cause" for the delay. He said it was the result of a "cumulative effect". "I do think they are not proceeding at the pace that would be in the best interests of energy consumers in New South Wales," Professor Christopher said. Ty Christopher spent decades delivering electricity infrastructure in NSW. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) In 2025-26, EnergyCo had just over $1 billion to build the zones, but spent $686 million. The year before, in its first year as a standalone agency, it spent $885 million of a $1.44 billion budget. Over the two years it has spent $939 million less than allocated, more than a third of its budget. An EnergyCo spokesperson said the gap between budgeted and actual spending "reflects the timing of project milestones, procurement and construction activities, and [is] not a direct measure of REZ delivery progress". Capacity: 6GW initial with potential to reach 8GW by 2034. The largest zone, legislated to account for two-thirds of the state's generation target. Still in planning, the environmental impact statement for the revised transmission corridor is due in late 2026. The tender for a network operator to build the transmission lines is expected to close at the end of 2027. The state's first and most advanced zone, currently in the delivery phase. The first transmission tower was erected in April 2026, and about $25 billion in private investment is expected. Network operator ACEREZ apologised after an Indigenous rock shelter was destroyed in May 2026 during land clearing for transmission lines. Work on the 700-kilometre transmission line connecting the NSW, Victoria and South Australian grids was completed in June 2026. In August, the NSW government confirmed $225 million to convert the Dinawan substation and transmission lines to 500 kV in preparation for the renewable projects associated with the REZ. Work in this zone involves upgrading existing power infrastructure in Newcastle and the Central Coast. There are three coal-fired power stations within the zone, including Eraring, Australia's largest coal-fired power station. Stage one of the upgrades was completed in May 2026, and the next phase will connect major regional hubs. The NSW government announced the Illawarra would become the state's first urban REZ after delays to large generation projects such as offshore wind. The zone will now focus on rooftop and community solar and batteries. A community reference group convened in August 2026. Professor Christopher, now the director of the Energy Futures Network at the University of Wollongong, said the money could not flow until the transmission routes are settled with the communities they pass through. "If they haven't been able to lock in the line routes with local communities, they can't spend the money to buy the easements, or start procuring equipment and building the lines," he said. NSW Energy Minister Penny Sharpe's office said the amount of large-scale wind and solar operating in NSW had risen more than 80 per cent since the 2023 election. Its delivery agency, EnergyCo, is held up as a model for other states to follow . But according to the independent agency tasked with monitoring whether the state is on track to meet its energy goals, NSW needs to be moving a lot faster. NSW is 7.9 gigawatts (GW) short of its legislated target of 12GW by 2030, and the amount of renewable generation commissioned each year must nearly double to close the gap, according to the NSW Net Zero Commission's latest progress report. Most renewable projects proposed in NSW have drawn significant opposition. Transmission lines like this one in the Riverina have divided residents.

events.title: From clearer diagnoses to faster matching for clinical trials: How Singapore’s precision medicine sector is changing patient care
events.summary: With Enterprise Singapore’s support, these home-grown companies are scaling innovations for clinical use and expanding into overseas markets Dr Gideon Ho (right) co-founded HistoIndex, one of the Singapore companies moving precision medicine from research into clinical care. In early 2026, a 13-year-old girl and her family faced a worrying possibility: the liver she had received in a transplant as a baby might have deteriorated. Seeking an additional – and objective – assessment, her specialist turned to Singapore biotechnology company HistoIndex for a clearer answer. Its technology found only minimal scarring, bringing relief to the family. Behind that reassuring result were years of research to turn complex science into a tool doctors can now use. How precision medicine can improve disease assessment HistoIndex’s technology, the result of 16 years of hard work, helps doctors see how a disease is changing and whether a treatment is working. Drug companies can also use the technology to assess potential new medicines. The firm’s approach is rooted in precision medicine, which uses a person’s genes, environment, and lifestyle to guide disease prevention, diagnosis and treatment. HistoIndex’s Genesis200 imaging system can examine tissue without the usual staining process, helping doctors measure the extent of fibrosis. As HistoIndex moved from research to commercial use, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) supported the development and validation of its AI-powered analysis tools. Its co-founder and chief executive officer Dr Gideon Ho says: “EnterpriseSG’s support enabled us to strengthen the underlying AI analytics, test the approach using clinically relevant liver-biopsy datasets and evaluate its performance against established pathology standards.” That helped lay the groundwork for the company to take its technology overseas and widen its international clinical adoption and collaborations, as its solutions gained traction and became a standard of use today in the diagnosis of certain liver diseases. Today, among many other collaborations, HistoIndex partners Peking University and Mt Sinai Health System in New York, and its customer base has expanded to include 21 large pharmaceutical companies, 20 biotechnology companies, and 60 universities, hospitals and research institutes. It is now looking to take the next step: bringing its AI-powered diagnostic and prognostic tests into more hospitals, while growing its business in the US. How doctors can test cancer treatments before prescribing them What if doctors could see how a cancer patient might respond to different drugs before deciding on a treatment? Singapore-based Kyan Technologies is working to do just that. Its platform, Optim.AI, tests medicines on a patient’s cancer cells outside the body, then analyses the results to help doctors identify promising treatment options. Results are typically available within seven to 10 days. The technology was first developed in the US before research continued at the National University of Singapore (NUS) from 2013. Clinical studies began in 2016, before the work was commercialised through the launch of Kyan Technologies in 2022. By 2023, the technology had moved into commercial patient use in Singapore, after Kyan’s laboratory was licensed by the Ministry of Health and accredited by the College of American Pathologists. The laboratory has since supported tests from more than 10 countries and patients cared for by nearly 200 clinicians worldwide. At Kyan Technologies’ laboratory, cancer cells are exposed to different drug combinations outside the body to assess their response and help inform treatment decisions. Kyan’s journey reflects a broader shift in Singapore’s precision medicine sector, as more research makes its way out of laboratories into clinical and commercial use. The precision medicine sector is growing rapidly worldwide, with its value projected to rise from about $100 billion today to $266 billion by 2034. In Singapore, it forms part of the country’s $32 billion biomedical sciences industry, with further development being driven by Phase III of the National Precision Medicine programme, which began last year. Dr Clarice Chen, director of healthcare and biomedical at EnterpriseSG, says: “Advancements in genomics, AI and digital health are enabling more personalised, preventive and predictive care, making precision medicine one of the most significant growth areas in healthcare today. “EnterpriseSG is committed to partnering innovative local companies to co-develop and validate these solutions with industry and global healthcare partners, helping them commercialise globally and contribute to healthcare systems worldwide.” Kyan co-founder and chief executive officer Hugo Saavedra remembers a much younger precision medicine sector when the technology was being developed in the 2010s. “What is stronger today is the pathway from research to commercialisation,” he says.

events.title: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building
events.summary: The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump , multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building , which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle. The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building . Driving the news: Axios could not immediately confirm when the closure will happen or how long it will be. A resolution from the board, filed as evidence in the ongoing legal fight with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the Center, listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building." Zoom out: A second resolution filed on Monday listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building." It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump." Friction point: U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper blocked the center from closing earlier this year, finding that "the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" and "based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided presentation of information." But in that order, he said his injunction would not prevent "capital repair work," nor would it "categorically prohibit the Board from closing the Center should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion." Catch up quick: The renovation project would address issues like corrosion and rehabilitating the building's iconic theaters and Grand Foyer, Axios previously reported. The draft resolution proposes sending marquee events offsite, while continuing some programming at the REACH — an indoor–outdoor space. Beyond infrastructure renovations, Trump ally and board member Paolo Zampolli outlined his luxury vision for the space to Axios' Cuneyt Dil, including expanding the outdoor park to create a "concert hub," and building a marina. What we're watching: For now, those ideas aren't part of the board's resolution — but the center's future under Trump remains in flux, in part because of an ongoing legal challenge to the president's takeover. And while Trump allies position him as the center's financial savior, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales plunged after the board of trustees voted to name the center after him. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Security firm Infoblox shines light on malicious infrastructure lurking beneath illegal gambling sites Ukrainian lawyer's second career as a Conti coder earns him 4 years behind bars 5 days ago Anthropic cracks down on hijacked user accounts mining AI tokens 15 days ago Crooks push Mac malware through fake OpenAI Codex ads 22 days ago Crook hawks millions of records allegedly plundered from corporate Azure tenants August 17, 2026 Ransomware attacks spike as world distracted by AI August 7, 2026 If your employees are visiting Chinese-language gambling or adult sites, they may not just be wasting time and money, but potentially encountering serious malware hidden behind domains that look like mostly harmless entertainment at first glance. A report from Infoblox urges the security community to pay closer attention to these websites, because some double as command-and-control (C2) infrastructure for espionage and malware distribution. Zach Edwards, staff threat researcher at Infoblox, suggests security researchers and the media have ignored these sites because the story is complicated and confusing. Infoblox says it tracks about 1.7 million Chinese-language casino websites that facilitate illegal gambling. These support North Korean money laundering and tax avoidance, among other dubious activities. And these casino sites can be difficult to distinguish from one another. They tend to use variations of common templates in terms of design and function. Many operate like a legal casino would, just relying on the advantage of house odds to profit. While these sites provide illegal gambling and adult entertainment for online visitors from China and Asia, some rely on US cloud providers for computing infrastructure. "Major US hosting companies (Amazon, Microsoft, Cloudflare, and Google) continue to host infrastructure associated with these domains," the Infoblox report explains. "One likely explanation is account theft at those providers, a practice documented previously as 'infrastructure laundering.'" That refers to hosting companies like Funnull that have reportedly rented IP addresses from Amazon Web Services and Microsoft and made those resources available to clients carrying out illegal activities. According to a July 2026 report from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), disparate crime syndicates increasingly use common infrastructure for cybercrime, while online scams resulted in estimated losses of between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion in 2025 across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. A subset of casino sites offer scam gambling, or " scambling ." Visitors place bets but can't get their money out if they win. And then there's a subset of sites used by China-aligned threat groups. "China-aligned APT groups have been running the PeckBirdy framework since 2023, hiding their malware C2 domains inside low-quality Chinese-language casino websites," Infoblox said. PeckBirdy , as noted by Trend Micro researchers in January, is a script-based framework that attackers can load through compromised websites. In one campaign, attackers injected scripts into gambling sites that loaded PeckBirdy and displayed fake software update pages designed to entice victims to download malware. The problem is that each of these three types of sites, though they change frequently, looks similar. Infoblox notes that just over 3 percent of its enterprise customers resolved at least one PeckBirdy C2 domain. "The most important thing for defenders to do is stop ignoring casino domains," Infoblox argues. "An alert on a Chinese-language casino or adult domain that gets closed as an employee browsing violation is precisely the outcome the PeckBirdy operators are counting on. The decoy works because the dismissal is reasonable – these domains genuinely are, most of the time, exactly what they appear to be." Security analysts who review suspicious network contacts are advised to check whether these casino domains include malicious payloads before closing the review ticket.

events.title: US borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
events.summary: US government borrowing costs climbed to their highest level since 2007 after a jump in oil prices further fuelled concerns about inflation. The effective interest rate on US government bonds over 10 years, known as the 10-year Treasury yield, rose as high as 5.04% but has eased back since. Government bond yields have been rising globally for months, driven by worries that inflation caused by the oil price surge since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran will lead to higher interest rates. The US has been buying back bonds in a bid to drive the Treasury yield down, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling the intervention "successful". The global benchmark wholesale oil price rose to over $109 a barrel on Tuesday, up from around $86 at the end of August, after renewed concerns about Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil following rising tensions in the region . Investors are anticipating the US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will raise interest rates to combat the inflation caused by higher oil prices. However, US President Donald Trump opposes a rate hike, having long argued lower rates are great for boosting the economy. He fell out with Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell over his decision not to cut rates. Higher interest rates and inflation tend to drive up the yields bond investors demand on government borrowing. Bond yields can also be a sign of how much faith investors have in a given government, with a higher yield reflecting less confidence. Competition for debt from artificial intelligence (AI) firms is also driving up yields. Tech giants are borrowing massive piles of cash to build huge data centres. This raises interest rates on tech firm's debt which increases government bond yields in response. Carol Schleif, chief market strategist at BMO Wealth Management, said bond markets had been signalling for weeks that higher interest rates may be needed. While the rise in borrowing costs has been "orderly" this year, rather than sudden, she said rates could remain elevated if geopolitical tensions and high energy prices remain "front and center". events.title: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI
events.summary: 2026 midterm elections: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI Sep 15, 2026 | By Ginny Badanes, General Manager, Tech for Society, Microsoft As Americans prepare to vote this November, artificial intelligence is changing how many people find and understand election information. Some voters are deliberately turning to AI tools with questions about candidates, ballot measures, election procedures, and issues that matter to their communities. Others are encountering AI-generated summaries at the top of search results. In either case, AI is increasingly becoming a front door to election information. This shift is happening quickly. More than 30% of the U.S. working-age population now uses AI (Microsoft AI Diffusion Index, Q1 2026; Microsoft, AI Adoption Across the United States ) . These tools can help people understand complicated topics, compare information, and explore unfamiliar issues. But election information can also present some challenges for AI. It is highly local, changes quickly, and can be incomplete, contested, or stripped of essential context. The answer is not to steer voters away from AI, it is to help people use it wisely, particularly when the information may influence aspects of their voting experience, such as how, when, and where they cast their ballot. That is why, on National Voter Registration Day , a day when our brands and products come together to encourage civic participation , we’re launching the next phase of our voter education initiative, Check. Recheck. Vote . This year, the campaign will equip voters with practical AI literacy skills for the 2026 election season. We launched Check. Recheck. Vote. in 2024 to help voters recognize the risks posed by deceptive AI-generated content. Deepfakes and other deceptive media remain a serious concern. But in conversations with voters and election organizations, we are also hearing about a broader and more immediate challenge. Millions of people now encounter election information through AI-generated answers, and many are not sure how to determine whether those answers are current, complete, or reliable. The updated campaign gives voters three straightforward steps: Check the sources and citations behind an AI-generated answer. Look for where the information came from, who published it, and when it was last updated. Be cautious when an answer provides no sources. Recheck important details by visiting the original sources and comparing what other credible sources say. This is especially important for fast-changing or location-specific information. Vote based on current information from your state or local election website, including official guidance on registration, voting options, deadlines, and polling locations. At the center of the campaign is a new 75-second video that shows how an AI-generated answer can appear during an ordinary election-related search, explains where these answers can fall short, and offers simple steps voters can take before relying on them. The campaign website pairs the video with practical guidance and links to authoritative election resources, including state-by-state voting information and tools for educators. We are working with the National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS) and the National Association of State Election Directors (NASED) to scale the reach of this campaign across all fifty states and the territories and to point voters to accurate information directly from state and local election officials so they can participate with confidence. We believe that civics and voter education start well before a citizen is old enough to vote. That’s why we are also investing in efforts to extend AI voter literacy education in the classroom. The campaign website includes a classroom activity to help students examine how AI may shape the election information they encounter, practice verifying claims, and keep their own judgment at the center of the process. We are also amplifying our impact on this important issue by supporting the News Literacy Project . We’re also proud to announce today that, in partnership with iCivics, we are launching Village Square – a new Minecraft Education civic learning experience that helps students explore how communities make decisions and solve shared challenges. The game brings concepts such as dialogue, participation, and collective decision-making to life through immersive gameplay. Village Square gives educators and families an engaging, nonpartisan way to help young people practice listening to different perspectives, weighing trade-offs and working together to build stronger communities. Finally, we know that credible local reporting remains essential to informed civic participation, and that reporting is under strain in many communities. In Washington state, Microsoft is partnering with the Associated Press Fund for Journalism to expand election coverage for 10 local newsrooms operating 14 news websites. Participating newsrooms receive access to AP election results and race calls, vote tabulations, state-specific maps and graphics, and resources that help local journalists connect national and statewide developments to the communities they serve. The newsrooms represent communities from Seattle to Spokane and the Wenatchee Valley. Their work complements the reporting of the Associated Press, helping trusted, fact-based election coverage and results reach communities that might otherwise lack access. This investment reflects a broader reality. Voters need more than information. They need reliable sources that can provide context, ask hard questions, correct mistakes, and explain what national developments mean at the local level. Microsoft’s Support for the 2026 Midterms Voters aren’t the only ones navigating this AI moment, so are the people running campaigns and conducting elections, all while facing an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. Microsoft has long supported the security and resilience of campaigns and elections. In 2018, we launched AccountGuard to help political campaigns and democracy-focused organizations defend against cyberattacks, and during the 2024 election cycle we joined dozens of other technology companies in the Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections . Here’s how that commitment continues today: Equipping election officials. With The Elections Group, International IDEA, Ready for Tuesday and Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Lab, we launched the free, open-source AI + Elections Skills Hub : prompts, sample AI agents, and draft policies for responsible adoption. It’s already reached 1,000+ officials across 45 states. Strengthening cybersecurity. We’ve deployed Microsoft Sentinel to several state and local election offices for stronger threat detection, and we’re also supporting select election and political stakeholders with MDASH to find and fix software vulnerabilities faster. Countering bomb hoaxes.

events.title: Influencers use parliament house showcase to spruik controversial MONAT brand
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts DSA posted multiple pictures from the event, including this one showing Industry Minister Tim Ayres with MONAT's vice-president Jen Usher and a top sales representative. ( LinkedIn: Direct Selling Australia ) Under-fire multi-level-marketing company MONAT, accused of misleading selling practices, has used an industry showcase at Parliament House to promote its legitimacy. The inaugural showcase, hosted by industry body Direct Selling Australia, was held weeks after an ABC investigation into MONAT. Critics say Parliament House should not be used for commercial ventures and are calling for better oversight on who is allowed to host events in the halls of power. Representatives of a multi-level-marketing company accused of making misleading and exaggerated income and lifestyle claims have used an industry showcase at Parliament House in Canberra to tout its legitimacy and tell followers it has been "discussed in parliament". The Florida-born hair and skincare company MONAT has come under fire with allegations that its representatives are making embellished sales pitches to recruit women into the multi-level-marketing scheme — including flaunting new cars, trips to tropical locations, and the ability to work from anywhere — while 93 per cent of its sellers make little to no money. An Instagram story shows MONAT vice-president Jen Usher representing the company at the event. ( Instagram: jen_usher ) It has been investigated twice in the United States over misleading product and income claims, and the ACCC has been urged to investigate its Australian sellers over whether their practices breach consumer law . MONAT's social media claims have renewed serious concerns about hiring out Parliament House rooms for commercial purposes, and businesses using them to suggest parliamentary endorsement. A MONAT influencer writes about the importance of the showcase being held at Parliament House. ( Instagram: bek.sharma ) Hosted by Direct Selling Australia (DSA), the inaugural showcase came just two weeks after the ABC investigation. DSA is the national body representing network marketing companies like MONAT, which is a paying member. MONAT's vice-president and managing director of Australia and New Zealand, Jen Usher, sat on the board in 2024-2025. Ms Usher attended the event, alongside one of the company's top sellers, and both spruiked the event on their social media accounts. Six politicians were tagged in a DSA LinkedIn post as joining the event, including federal Minister for Industry and Innovation Tim Ayres. Mr Ayres declined to answer questions from the ABC. A post from one of the MONAT sellers saying MONAT was "discussed in parliament". ( Instagram: melissamunro._x ) Several MONAT representatives posted to their social media accounts to promote the showcase as a "powerful reminder that social selling is a legitimate, regulated industry". "Seeing our work discussed in parliament is a huge achievement," one representative wrote. "To see our industry being represented and having conversations inside Parliament House is pretty bloody cool," another wrote. Former NSW Supreme Court judge and chair of the Centre for Public Integrity, Anthony Whealy, said claiming legitimacy through presence in Parliament House was misleading. He said it was "not a good look" and asked whether Parliament House should be used for commercial purposes. Former NSW Supreme Court Judge Anthony Whealy questions whether Parliament House should be used for commercial ventures. ( ABC News ) Independent senator David Pocock said events at Parliament House should be used as a "force for good". "I do not believe parliamentary events should be used for fundraising or for the commercial benefit or endorsement of individual companies," he said. "Historically, there has been fairly poor oversight of the kind of events conducted inside Parliament House, and it is something I have pursued at Senate estimates and raised with the presiding officers. "I would be very uncomfortable having my photo used for promotional or endorsement purposes that I was not aware of or did not agree to." David Pocock says there needs to be better oversight of events conducted in Parliament House. ( ABC News: Adam Kennedy ) ABC's Four Corners recently highlighted these concerns, and whether stronger safeguards were needed around commercial interests and lobbying inside Parliament House. A statement from MONAT Global sent to the ABC by one of its Australian representatives said the company was "proud" to have been part of the event.

( Staunch by Senator Babet ) Senator Ralph Babet's new clothing line, which includes products carrying the Australian flag, was not made in Australia. In his first speech, the senator advocated support for local manufacturing, but said the clothes were made overseas because it was too expensive to do so in Australia. Senator Babet has flagged his intention to retire when his term expires in 2028. "Christian nationalist" Senator Ralph Babet's new fashion line, which includes Australian flag towels, mugs and socks, is made in South America and Asia. The lone United Australia Party senator launched "Staunch by Senator Babet" this month, a line that carries shirts with political and religious slogans. Among them are shirts depicting the senator smoking a cigar, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with the caption "zero testosterone detected", a shirt featuring "the world is controlled by Satanic paedophiles", as well as shirts with biblical references. The ABC contacted the support line for Senator Babet's clothing brand and was told that the products were mostly made in South America and Asia, and then sent to the United States or another country for screen printing. Senator Babet confirmed the products were manufactured offshore, with screen printing done in Australia. After the ABC spoke directly with Senator Babet, a new T-shirt design appeared on his website calling to "defund the ABC", which notes that other parties and senators also sell merchandise. Staunch by Senator Babet added this design after the ABC spoke with the senator about his clothing line. ( Staunch by Senator Babet ) Senator Babet entered parliament on a platform of putting Australia "first", and in his first speech to parliament called on Australians and the parliament to support local manufacturing. "We must become a nation which makes things again. Our manufacturing sector has been decimated and sent offshore, once again at the behest of unelected global bureaucrats. Let's take the brakes off our businesses and entrepreneurs. Let them work. Let them produce. Let them create wealth," Senator Babet said in 2022. "We need to ensure that we give Australian businesses strong support and an unencumbered legislative pathway so they can grow, compete and become major players on the world stage." Senator Babet told the ABC he was not using an Australian manufacturer because it was cheaper to make clothing overseas, and high taxes and energy costs made it prohibitive to manufacture onshore. "If you can find a T-shirt manufacturer in Australia, I would use them, but there isn't one," Senator Babet said. "These days everything is made in China." Staunch by Senator Babet sells products carrying the Australian flag, including this towel, though the products are not manufactured in Australia. ( Staunch by Senator Babet ) Senator Babet has recently used clips of his speeches to the Senate to promote his brand on social media, with for-sale shirts and links to his website overlaid on videos where he advocates for more limited government. But he told the ABC the fashion line was a personal project and self-funded, with no parliamentary resources used on the brand. His fashion project would not support the United Australia Party but instead would go towards advertising for causes he supported, such as lowering migration. The senator said it had not yet been declared because 'Staunch' was not yet making enough money to warrant formal disclosure. Labor attacks attendance record of 'Ghost of the Senate' In February, Senator Babet announced he would not re-contest his position when his term expired in 2028, saying he had "failed" as a senator to protect free speech. Senator Babet was the only successful candidate who ran under Clive Palmer's United Australia Party banner at the 2022 election, despite the mining billionaire spending $117 million on that campaign through his company Mineralogy. Ralph Babet was elected as a senator for Victoria in 2022 under Clive Palmer's United Australia Party banner. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) On Monday, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher taunted the senator over his attendance in the Senate, after his question was handed to One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts to be asked. "I think that's the second week in a row you've had Senator Babet's question. You lucky guy! I wonder where the ghost of the Senate is," Senator Gallagher said. "We never see him anymore, do we? I noticed he did launch a clothing range a few days ago though, so he had time to do that.

events.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
events.summary: President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use. Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers. The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue. Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position." Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads." Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources. Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies. "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday. Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates. First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use. Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities. Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water. "The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside." Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource demands are known. By the numbers: Fabrizio's polling shows voters are far more receptive to data center construction with conditions than unrestricted development. Sixty-one percent of registered voters favor allowing construction with conditions, compared with 28% who favor prohibiting data centers altogether. His polling also finds voters oppose additional data center construction without conditions by 65% to 24%. The background: Fabrizio is a central player in Trump's midterm political operation, helping shape the polling and strategy guiding the GOP's campaign to retain control of Congress. Yes, but: Trump remains an enthusiastic booster of data centers even as Republicans grapple with growing voter concerns about their local impact. "I'm telling you, it's all a hoax. The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy, and it's the oil of the next 20, 25 years," Trump said Monday.

events.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely on Monday. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. Relay — a startup outpaced by bigger platforms — is one version of the story playing out right now. But plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

events.title: Suncorp's debt collector engaging in 'worst kind' of bullying, former ACCC chair says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Diane and Scott Walker spent months fighting an insurance claim they likened to "bullying". ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Debt collector ARMA Group spent months harassing and intimidating 81-year-old Diane Walker into paying an insurance claim she was not responsible for. ARMA, acting on behalf of insurance giant Suncorp, ended the ordeal with an apology to Ms Walker and financial compensation for the distress caused, but only after months of legal threats and pressure to pay. "They were rather bullying-type letters … it's in the back of your mind all the time," Ms Walker said. ARMA's website says its workflows are "AI-driven", boasting it takes the company "less than two minutes to set up a smart payment plan and no manual intervention is required". Ms Walker's case is just the tip of the iceberg as the consumer watchdog takes ARMA Group and Force Legal, both owned by Credit Clear Limited, to court, alleging that between them they sent 320,000 debt enforcement notices to individuals that were allegedly misleading. Former ACCC chair Allan Fels says he is "very concerned" about the conduct of debt collector ARMA Group. ( ABC News: Patrick Rocca ) Legal experts are appalled and say it is a clear breach of Australian consumer laws. "This is Robodebt 2.0 of the worst form," said Allan Fels, former chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC). "I'm very concerned … this seems to be the worst kind of illegal, deceptive conduct applied to bully, intimidate, frighten. "It's traumatic for the individual to be confronted in a Robodebt situation with no opportunity to respond or fight back, or talk to someone, or explain their personal circumstances. "There needs to be a serious, substantial crackdown on this kind of approach." If you have more information about this article or any other tips, you can securely contact reporter Adelaide Miller at miller.adelaide@proton.me Just before Christmas, Ms Walker was involved in a minor two-vehicle car crash she was not responsible for, and that caused no damage. Diane Walker was sent multiple legal threats for a car insurance claim she was never liable for. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The other driver's insurer, AAMI, a subsidiary of Suncorp, contacted Ms Walker looking to recover costs, despite having no evidence. "I would have emailed them at least half a dozen times saying, 'Send me some photos, send me something that demonstrates that at least something happened,'" said Scott Walker, who stepped in as his mother's representative on the claim. About two months after AAMI first contacted Ms Walker, it engaged its debt collector, ARMA Group, to recover the funds. Without providing evidence, the debt collector concluded that Ms Walker was "liable". Previously a freelance camera operator for the ABC, Mr Walker said he spent hundreds of hours trying to make sense of ARMA's communication. "It was just this level of intimidation … the wording sounded very much like there's been some legal decision made, some type of independent, judicial system that has found an outcome," he said. Ms Walker and her son said ARMA's letters were relentless. Despite initially telling Ms Walker she had been found "liable" for the car accident, ARMA began threatening court action, suggesting culpability remained unresolved. One letter said: "If you choose to dispute the issue with arguments that are not relevant — such as claiming there is no dashcam footage or no photos of the vehicles at the moment of impact — we will have no choice but to escalate the matter further. "You are welcome to present those arguments in court if you believe they support your case. If you are found liable, you would be liable for court fees as well." ARMA Group was initially claiming $1,175.51 from Ms Walker. But after three months, the company increased the amount to $1,395.51 without explanation. Mr Walker was then sent a separate claim, arguing he was now responsible for the accident, even though he wasn't there at the time. Scott Walker says he spent hundreds of hours on the insurance claim before receiving an apology. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "The system's not designed to have a sensible conversation with someone at the other end; it's a system that is designed to make you pay," Mr Walker said. ARMA Group did not respond to questions from ABC News. Suncorp did not provide an on the record response to the ABC's questions. The number of Australians with debt is rising sharply, with contact to the National Debt Help Line increasing by nearly 12 per cent in the year to August.

events.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
events.summary: Data: The Economist/YouGov ; Chart: Avery Lotz A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive. The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war , tariffs or other top priorities . Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency . By the numbers: " Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters. Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%). Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president. Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high , per Gallup's trend , and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office. The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans. Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion. Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars." Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government. Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend , this month. Some 35% of Americans approved of his performance, up from 33% in the late August poll, per Reuters. Between the lines: The last thing many Republicans want, Axios' Marc Caputo reports , is for Trump to make the midterms a vote on his popularity (or lack thereof). Still, Trump headlined both nights of the party's midterm convention in Dallas and pledged a $5,000 dividend to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans keep control of Congress — a plan that would cost more than $1 trillion. Friction point: YouGov's polling found that a majority signaled they believe it's unlikely Trump actually follows through with the idea, which Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has said would require congressional approval. More than four in 10 (41%) said he definitely wouldn't do it, while an additional 16% said he probably wouldn't. More said it was a bad idea (45%) than those who said it was a good idea (38%). Methodology: This Economist-sponsored poll was taken September 11-14, 2026. Respondents were selected from YouGov's opt-in panel to be representative of adult U.S. citizens, and screened for voter registration. The margin of error is ± 3.3%. events.title: Microsoft’s partners debut new Windows PCs at IFA
events.summary: More choice and possibility with Windows PCs at IFA Mark Linton, Corporate Vice President, Windows & Devices This year at IFA, I saw the Windows ecosystem doing what it does best: bringing innovation to life through products and experiences for every person, purpose, and price point. Our partners introduced new Windows PCs, spanning dependable everyday devices, beautifully crafted premium designs, new and immersive gaming systems, commercial devices designed to help organizations work securely and productively, and powerful tools for developers, creators, and AI power users. Together, these announcements demonstrated the breadth of what’s possible with a Windows PC. This matters because people are being thoughtful about when, where, and how they spend. We know that a new PC is a meaningful purchase, and that customers want to feel confident that they choose the right PC for them. They want to know that it will deliver a better experience today while continuing to meet their needs for years to come. Windows PCs from our partners give people more ways to find the right device without compromising on what matters most to them. For more than 40 years, our goal has been to put a computer on every desk and in every home. We know the PC is personal and the place you go to play, create, build, connect and learn. Some prioritize battery life and portability, while others need greater performance for gaming or creative work. And increasingly, people are also looking for useful AI experiences that are easy to use and fit seamlessly into their existing workflows. And of course, everyone needs to find the right device at the right price for them. IFA showed how our partners are meeting those different needs. The strength of Windows is choice, and the latest Windows PCs bring together modern design, stronger performance, built-in security and useful AI experiences available at different price points. For those who have been holding on to an older PC, the choice and value available today makes it a good time to find the right device. IFA also demonstrated how Windows is evolving for the next era of computing. The latest OpenClaw Windows App makes it easier to configure and run AI models locally on supported NV IDIA RTX Spark Windows PCs. It builds on the secure agent-execution foundation we introduced at Microsoft Build, helping agents work within defined boundaries while taking advantage of the computing power available on the device. We are also making it easier for developers to turn ideas into reality with new ready-to-code Windows experiences for next-generation devices. By pre -installing the essential tools and pre-configuring Windows settings for development on developer class devices with 64GB+ unified memory and 250gbps memory bandwidth, developers can jump right in . Project Zenith devices enable developers to run capable coding models locally and unmetered, helping lower token costs , experiment more freely, and stay in their flow. events.title: US data centers could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt The AI race has grown so frenzied that, by 2035, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined. Over the next decade, data centers are expected to be the second-strongest driver of natural gas demand growth after LNG exports. The facilities could consume about 18 billion cubic feet per day, according to a new report from BloombergNEF , nearly double the amount the organization predicted just nine months ago. The new forecast takes into account that not all announced data center projects will be completed. Data centers that produce power onsite have grabbed headlines in recent months, with Meta , Microsoft , Google , and Amazon all announcing plans for new natural gas power plants that will bypass the grid. Projects such as these will consume 2.9 billion to 3.4 billion cubic feet per day by 2035. That’s about as much as all data centers consume today , including natural gas used to generate power for the grid. But onsite-powered data centers could represent just a fraction of overall demand growth, according to BloombergNEF. By the middle of the next decade, grid-connected data centers are predicted to drive an additional 15 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas consumption by the power sector. To put that in context, that’s five times more demand growth through 2035 than from all other grid-connected sectors combined. If that stunning demand growth materializes, it could nudge natural gas prices higher. Much of today’s data center buildout relies on stable natural gas prices, which have prevailed in recent years. But analysts at Noreva think that might be a false hope. The combined impact of the data center boom and rising LNG exports could cause prices to soar . Even if tech companies’ balance sheets can bear such a surge, utility ratepayers might not be able to. Burning one cubic foot of natural gas releases the equivalent of 60 grams of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, including extraction, processing, and distribution, according to the IEA. The additional demand from data centers will generate 1 million metric tons more greenhouse gas pollution daily. That’s about 12% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions today.
